items.body:
Over the course of the last decade, the group أحمد [Ahmed] has carved out a distinctive approach to the jazz canon through their tireless exploration of the music of Ahmed Abdul-Malik. Mining Abdul-Malik’s compositions and his incorporation of non-Western microtonality into the jazz vocabulary, pianist Pat Thomas, alto saxophone player Seymour Wright, bassist Joel Grip, and drummer Antonin Gerbal have done more than reinterpretation. They have used the music as a foundation for both immersion and subversion of the way that the standard jazz quartet functions within post-bop structures. For last year’s Sama'a (Audition), they went into the studio for an expansive refraction of Abdul-Malik’s Jazz Sahara. During that same session, the four took a slight detour to record Play Monk, a dive into deconstructions of six pieces by Thelonious Monk, all but one of which he recorded in the late 1950s when Abdul-Malik was part of his group. أحمد [Ahmed] has incorporated Monk tunes into their live sets but this is the first time they have focused on his tunes on a recording.

While Thomas, Wright, Grip, and Gerbal have not altered their strategies in the switch of source material, there is one significant shift in the way one listens to this music. A quick search returns no other versions of Abdul-Malik’s pieces other than those recorded by the composer or أحمد [Ahmed] whereas Monk’s “Epistrophy” or “’Round Midnight” have hundreds. Even a less well-known piece like “Oska T” has dozens. Because the pieces covered are so well known, their teasing apart and restructuring of the underlying thematic kernels are more readily evident. Over two CDs, the quartet digs in, with improvisations that range between 20 and 30 minutes with the exception of a seven-minute extrapolation of “Epistrophy.” These extended explorations allow the group to excavate the forms with a focused patience, zeroing in on and elucidating microscopic details, extricating them into the fundamental elements of penetrating improvisations.

The first phrases of the opening “Bye-ya / Epistrophy” provide a glimpse of what is to come. Bass and piano circle around the theme and Gerbal’s lithe drumming circles up to drive momentum. Wright’s stabbing alto picks apart the melody and the four launch off on a circuitous inquiry, dismantling Monk’s tune into its constituent fragments and then reassembling them with constructivist abstraction. Each of the four seize on elements of the underlying piece, playing them off of each other with unwavering resolve, an approach the group continues to advance in their sweeping live sets. There is an insistent intensity as Wright’s notes pick and prod at Thomas’ skewed clusters, Grip’s free walking lines, and Gerbal’s churning free rhythms. Shards of “Epistrophy” are introduced into the mix by Grip and Thomas, slowly accruing with multifaceted erudition.

The group continues to subvert expectations with “Friday the Thirteenth” as Thomas insistently repeats the first phrase of the tune against Grip’s growling arco inversions. Wright’s keypad pops and Gerbal’s open percussion build momentum and Wright unleashes spattered honks that open into a collective four-part splintering of the theme, picking it apart and recasting it with angular exactitude, building density and intensity over the course of the sweeping 26-minute improvisation. “’Round Midnight” gets a relatively straightforward introduction with Wright intoning the theme over sinuous bass and cymbal splashes. Thomas’ spare chords enter as the quartet dynamically transposes the constituent parts of the piece with imperturbable resolution resolving with the riveting cycling hushed snare abrasions that brings the piece to a close.

A seven-minute scorching, stuttering run through “Epistrophy” serves as an interlude to an abstracted, cascading reading of “Evidence” which takes Monk’s stop-start theme and explodes it with relentless, spiraled piano phrases and the hurtling momentum of bass and drums driving Wright’s coruscating alto which prods and jabs with spiky dexterity. The 30-minute improvisation is an engulfing exemplification of unflagging invention. Monk’s “Oska T.,” structured around an obsessively cyclical riff, is a fitting conclusion to the release. The quartet slows things down to a free shuffle with bass and alto arcing over the mutable pulse of piano and drums. The four players adroitly weave their lines in and out of the collective undercurrent with indefatigable ingenuity. While others have dedicated themselves to the reinterpretation of the music of Thelonious Monk, أحمد [Ahmed]’s Play Monk is distinctive in its mastery, fully absorbing his music into the collective rigor and artistry of this singular ensemble.
items.label: Otoroku ROKU047
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以塞隆尼斯·蒙克的六首曲目为素材，是四人组在录制上一张专辑同期完成的延伸计划。他们没有沿用标准爵士四重奏的独奏加伴奏模式，而是把原曲拆成碎片，以萨克斯、钢琴、贝斯和鼓彼此挤压与回应。评论指出，由于蒙克这些作品广为流传，这种拆解、放大和重组比他们此前处理阿卜杜勒-马利克作品时更容易被识别。多数段落长达二十至三十分钟，仅一首七分钟，乐队以接近耐心的方式反复挖掘主题的微观细节，让动机残片在自由即兴中持续积累。节奏与和声结构被松散重构，演奏保持高度专注和紧张感，适合关注自由即兴与爵士解构的听者。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.
items.label: Cool Waters
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由德国出生的肯尼亚打击乐手Sven Kacirek与肯尼亚歌手Ogoya Nengo、Olith Ratengo合作完成。83岁的Nengo与Ratengo以传统dodo演唱相互呼应，Kacirek则以Buchla合成器、手打击乐和鼓组构建电子声场。作品以重复节奏为基底，逐渐叠加多层合成器复节奏，如《Bara》从机械节拍演化出贝斯与木琴质感；《Sarah》则在人声高潮处加入失真，强化紧迫感。音乐在技术与人声之间保持平衡，既保留肯尼亚传统根源，又融入当代电子实验，呈现全球文化交流中传统与创新的相互渗透，而非简单拼贴或覆盖。

items.album: Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari
items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Dorothy Moskowitz与作曲家Francesco Paolo Paladino、诗人Luca Chino Ferrari合作的十一首作品。音乐以钢琴为核心，时而交错相位，辅以弦乐、木管与合成器声墙，呈现出非线性和调性模糊的质感，明显受到Steve Reich、Philip Glass等简约主义作曲家的影响，挑战了熟悉的和谐进行。歌词兼具诗意与直接的政治性，如《Pale Wanderer》讨论极权需要共谋，《Charlottesville》以近年新纳粹集会为背景，延续60年代抗议歌曲的精神，同时渗透对死亡与人类位置的沉思。Moskowitz的演唱带有经验与疲倦的叙述感，像方法派演员般赋予文字重量，钢琴则作为另一重声部乃至希腊歌队参与叙事。整张专辑在实验声响与人文关怀之间取得平衡，既非纯粹的抽象声音实验，也非传统歌曲结构，而是让形式与内容相互支撑，在当下动荡时局中重新激活了前卫音乐的批判功能。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items.body: The year of blue continues: blue art, blue music, blue moods. Klara Lewis‘ Opening is an azure version of the hue, twisting and turning like permutations seen beneath varying degrees of light. The first single and opening track “Ta Min Hand” establishes the baseline from which the album will drift, like a small vessel upon the sea. Even the music includes waves. A sweet melody emerges, loops and abrades. In “City,” solo piano plays over the sounds of traffic and conversation, momentarily pausing as if to listen to the other acoustic sources. Suddenly a more aggressive set of sounds conquers the sonic field, a helicopter of rovers and gears. The piano reenters, insistent, then the conversation, posing questions about where the attention turns in an economy of sonic competition. The more orchestral “Vaknar” (“Waking”) attempts to soothe, but the ground has already proven unstable. The looping continues, but the volume increases. Opening revels in juxtaposition and incremental shift. “Feel” and “Drip” were composed for Mika Taanila’s expressive film “Failed Emptiness,” which toys with expectations of light. As the album’s most abrasive piece, “Feel” stands in contrast to the melodies that haunt the earlier selections. The brief “Drip” is its polar opposite, nearly a dance piece, restricted only by its length, the connecting tissue a feedback drone emerging toward the end. “Tide,” by far the album’s longest piece at 11:37, is dedicated to Christine Ödlund’s painting “Dissolving Strawberry,” and is also on a compilation EP that finds connections between pigment and tone. While listening, one gleans melodies through gauze, origins obscured like fragments of forgotten lyrics. By “How Far?” abstraction begins to win over form, Lewis’ voice suddenly emerging in the center as another instrument. Furthering the sense of inversion, the set closer is called “Opening,” making one wonder if the title may mean an opening, such as a pathway or door; or the sense of opening one’s self to unpredictability or the divine. By the time the album ends, one has been led down multiple pathways, and even the trail of string has become tangled. To find one’s bearings, one must return to the beginning or plunge further into the unknown. (Richard Allen)

items._cn_summary: Klara Lewis 的专辑《Opening》以蓝色为意象核心，将环境氛围、噪音与旋律线相互渗透。专辑建立在循环结构之上，开篇曲以海浪般的波动铺设基调，钢琴段落穿插于城市交通与人声采样之间，探讨声音空间中注意力的竞争关系。中段作品源自为影像创作，呈现极端对比：一首以刺耳噪音为主体，另一首则近乎舞曲片段却被极短时长所限制。最长的曲目长达十一分钟，旋律被纱幕般的音色层所遮蔽，来源模糊如同遗忘的歌词碎片。终曲回归专辑同名，以开放性收尾，暗示多重路径的并行可能。整张专辑在旋律与抽象之间反复游走，体现出对声响材料与艺术跨界合作的深入思考。

items.body: Review by omphaloskepsis — When I picture the Mount Rushmore of Chamber Prog, I clearly see the colossal Universe Zero and Present rising above a foggy valley, carved into the mountain side. The thick mist of time obscures the other etched visages jutting from the far-side of the Mountain. The Fool Leading The Blind amazes me and I wonder..."Will Asceta approach Univers Zero and Present's greatness? Time will tell. Asceta's album The Fool Leading the Blind is a resplendent, melodic, and focused masterpiece of modern chamber rock and Rock in Opposition (RIO). The epic tapestry, fashioned by multi-instrumentalist and composer Rodrigo Maccioni, the Chilean ensemble crafts an intricate sound shroud knit together with awesome, seamless transitions. Bassoon, clarinets, viola, and English horn merge with a jazzy electric guitars, bass, and drums. Asceta's music doesn't percolate with as many dissonate passages as Univers Zero or Present. Don't get me wrong, Asceta sails through its share of breathtaking dissonate rapids. However, Asceta's The Fool Leading The Blind seems more focused on melodic movements...much like classical compositions from a couple centuries ago.The Title Suite: The opening 21-minute epic flows fluidly from eerie, atmospheric sound spheres to exhilarating crescendos. The dynamic Interplay of tracks like Temple of Mirrors and When They Arrive showcase tight counterpoints where no single instrument dominates, weaving impeccable sonic tapestries into complex patterns. Every track is a treat! Asceta's thought-provoking, sonic bouquet shimmers like shattered stain glass in a cathedral on fire. Highly recommended for lovers of Univers Zero and Present.

items.body: Of course, this trio is a supergroup, like so many of pianist Vijay Iyer’s latest ensembles. Percussionist Dafnis Prieto may be less well-known, but the now 82-year-old saxophonist and flutist Henry Threadgill is all the more so. Despite his age, he has been more productive and acclaimed than ever. He won the Pulitzer Prize for his most important work of the past 15 years, In for a Penny, In for a Pound (Zooid; 2015). It’s possibly the most consistent realization of Threadgill’s compositional system, in which he works with predetermined interval sequences that provide the musicians with a harmonic and melodic framework within which they are also expected to improvise - that is, improvisation itself becomes part of a highly complex composition. What’s fascinating about this is that the music initially seems almost chaotic, but is in fact organized with extraordinary precision. As intellectually fascinating as this music is on the one hand, it has also faced criticism on the other hand, that the whole thing is too contrived and too lifeless, too close to new classical avant-garde music. That kind of criticism can certainly not applied to “Fifteen”. The album title refers to the number of years that have passed since this trio first came together at a benefit event for the New York Jazz Gallery. Here, all three compose and improvise; recurring melodic patterns are readily - even eagerly - embraced, bringing the music closer to mainstream jazz than to free jazz. This is primarily due to Dafnis Prieto’s Cuban influences and his light, elastic groove, which remains free and almost impossible to count. This is perhaps most clearly evident in “I Want a Map”, which comes across more like a rock song, with Threadgill’s saxophone initially taking up the melody, which is developed by the piano and built up relatively straightforwardly by the drums to a crescendo. Rarely has Threadgill sounded so accessible; he uses a fair amount of growl, and his clear sound from the Air years is barely recognizable. But he wouldn’t be Henry Threadgill if he didn’t gradually incorporate small atonal elements and offbeat shifts that disrupt the piece’s static structure. Things get significantly wilder on “Fire City“, then. Prieto plays less to the beat. Here, he actually acts more like a free jazz drummer. Iyer, too, plays fewer tonal harmonies, and Threadgill’s sound is indeed clearer and more abstract on this track. The piece is denser, less airy than others on the album, but perhaps that’s precisely what makes it the most exciting, as it gallops off in different directions several times without ever losing its way. The most unusual track is the album’s finale, “On the Way”. Here, the different compositional and improvisational logics stand in direct contrast to one another: Henry Threadgill’s carefully balanced vocabulary meets the rhythmic power and temporal sophistication of Iyer and Prieto, opening up spaces for dense ensemble polyrhythms and incisive solo passages. At times, you can literally tap your foot along - you almost feel like dancing. Who would ever have expected that from an album featuring Henry Threadgill? This is definitely one of the albums that will appear on many year-end charts. Fifteen is available on vinyl, as a CD and as a download. You can listen to it and buy it on Vijay Iyer’s bandcamp site: Fifteen by Henry Threadgill, Vijay Iyer, Dafnis Prieto Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._genre: free jazz / avant-garde / improvisation / contemporary composition
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由萨克斯/长笛演奏家Henry Threadgill、钢琴家Vijay Iyer和打击乐手Dafnis Prieto组成的三重奏呈现，标题致敬三人十五年前首次合作的慈善演出。三位音乐家各自贡献作曲与即兴，旋律模式被频繁使用，使整体风格偏向主流爵士而非自由爵士。Prieto的弹性古巴律动贯穿全作，在《I Want a Map》中呈现近似摇滚的推进方式。Threadgill虽已82岁，却展现出罕见的可亲近性，咆哮般的萨克斯音色与早年Air时期的清亮大相径庭，但他仍巧妙融入小规模无调性元素打破静态结构。《Fire City》转向更密集的探索，鼓手脱离节拍束缚，钢琴减少调性铺垫，三人以自由爵士方式对话，作品多次在张力释放中保持方向感。终曲《On the Way》中，三人的作曲与即兴逻辑直接碰撞，构建出密集合奏多节奏群与锐利独奏段落并置的空间。

items.body: Honoring its title, Justyna Jablonska‘s Unforeseen never heads exactly where expected; in fact, it’s not even close. The cellist’s debut solo album drips with the confidence of exploration, incorporating multiple genres while acting as a metaphor for the immigrant experience. Jablonska connects the migration of birds with the migration of people and the migration of oft-improvised notes, focusing on the lives of Ukrainian, Polish and Roma Gypsy migrants. While this seems like a lot to tackle, the artist does so with aplomb. The album begins as one might expect a cellist’s album to begin, with sedate phrasing, multitracked lines and a regal tone. The title track demonstrates Jablonska’s depth of emotion while establishing the baseline from which it will soon wander. Were the record to have continued in this vein, it would have remained exemplary; yet the artist strives for something greater, just as those dreaming for a better life might pack their belongings, imitating the flocks passing overhead in the spring and fall. As “If You Can Hear This” launches with a spoken word sample and jungle rhythms, all bets are off. The artist will not be confined by expectation. Is it safe? Not at all, and therein lies the appeal. The bird, the immigrant, the artist may each be called upon to adapt to new surroundings. “9 Daughers” is the first of three vocal pieces, beginning in birdsong and proceeding to a rendition of a traditional Lithuanian folk song A linden tree has nine branches, each one corresponding to a daughter, who each in turn are married, leaving the mother to “sweep the ashes.” The tone is one of mingled celebration and sadness: the empty nest, the broken tree. Can even the birds sing the sorrow away? The next piece starts with the sound of traffic, implying movement; then peaceful kalimba, cello and electronics, each in turn moving the music further away from its origins. The skies open in “Wayward,” and Jablonska seems forlorn, until a series of upbeat melodies are translated to percussion and string. These are the unforeseen joys of leaving the place where one has begun; by the end, the skies have cleared. But not all changes are easy; “Fabryka” introduces a brief note of dissonance, setting the listener up for Monika Niemczynowicz’s return on “The Pact,” an extremely dark cautionary tale from Roztocze, Poland. The presence of such songs underlines the connection between land, culture and memory ~ tales passed down generation to generation, even when the family has migrated to a new home. One hungers for the live show, incorporating film and copious amounts of spoken word, hinted at in the final minute of “Procession.” The album’s greatest surprise arrives toward the end with “Shchedryk (feat. Sofiia Fylypiv).” Most listeners will recognize “Carol of the Bells” in an instant, and many will recall its Ukrainian origins, but few will remember that the song predates Christianity and is about a swallow wishing a family “prosperity, good fortune and a fruitful year.” Jablonska reinstates the original title and meaning, reclaiming it from distortion. This too is a metaphor for the immigrant experience: the temptation to integrate to the extent that one’s history is sublimated. Jablonska, who lives in Glasgow, closes with her own take on “The Skye Boat Song,” which was itself adapted from a Gaelic tune. By the end, one is wondering about the the tug between one’s national origin and country of residence, and the very definition of home. (Richard Allen)
items._genre: contemporary classical / experimental / world fusion / electronic
items._cn_summary: 大提琴家Justyna Jablonska首张个人专辑以"迁徙"为核心隐喻，将鸟类迁徙、移民经验与即兴音符的流动并置，聚焦乌克兰、波兰与罗姆吉普赛移民议题。开篇以稳健的多轨大提琴声部奠定古典底色，随后迅速突破预期：丛林节奏、spoken word采样、卡林巴铁琴、电子声响与立陶宛民谣交织，三首人声作品在鸟鸣与古老叙事的悲喜之间游走。既有传统民谣的转译，也有工业质感的实验编排，末尾以乌克兰经典"Shchedryk"（铃儿响叮当）作惊喜收束。整张专辑在当代古典、电子实验与世界音乐之间自由穿行，文化记忆与声音探索相互渗透，展现出强烈的跨界意识与艺术野心。

items.body: On Islands Alight, percussion takes on a structural role, the bass gains weight, echo intervenes in the form, and the pulse alters the relationship between the different parts. The British composer points to the history of dub within electronic music as one of the project’s sources. Entrusting rhythm with a greater share of the tension Islands Alight by James Murray   James Murray arrives at this work after a path in which restraint has become an aesthetic choice even before a technical one. For years, his electronic music has pursued a precise relationship between duration, timbre, and memory. He favors slow construction, minimal variation, and change that acquires meaning over time. The new album brings this approach into more rhythmic territory, shifting the center of gravity of his writing. The transition feels significant precisely because of how naturally it occurs. Murray has long worked with minimal electronic and electroacoustic forms, dense with detail and shaped by a strong awareness of sound. On Islands Alight, percussion takes on a structural role, the bass gains weight, echo intervenes in the form, and the pulse alters the relationship between the different parts. The British composer points to the history of dub within electronic music as one of the project’s sources. It is the most appropriate reference through which to understand this aspect of the album: a culture of space, listening, and studio transformation absorbed into a personal body of research. Four years of work have produced a cohesive record. Continuity is one of its greatest strengths. The London-based musician prefers to work with relationships, allowing an element to change function through what surrounds it. A rhythmic figure gains incisiveness through a minimal shift. A harmonic sequence recedes, allowing a previously secondary detail to emerge. The control is rigorous and almost always discreet. This economy is part of his poetics. Murray places value on restraint, listening, attention to detail, and trust in the person receiving the music. Islands Alight translates these principles into a very concrete form. Passages are given the time they need to develop their function. Resolutions are postponed. Gratification often arrives only after an extended period within the same sonic field, once the relationship between the elements has already altered perception. “Echo alters the memory of what has just happened. Low frequencies establish weight and continuity. Percussion introduces pressure. The synthesizers retain the emotional quality that has long characterized his work. Together, these elements produce music that remains unmistakably his.” ~Mirco Salvadori Rhythm changes this dynamic considerably. It introduces a more pronounced physical dimension and makes the music more mobile. Percussion guides the listening experience with an elastic presence. The pulse moves forward, thins out, then returns with a different weight. Bass affects both depth and the perception of time. Delay and reverb organise distance, duration, and density. The effects belong to the composition just as much as the harmonic parts do. The relationship with the history of dub can be measured above all through this method. Murray takes certain production principles and brings them into his own language. The studio becomes part of the writing process. Echo alters the memory of what has just happened. Low frequencies establish weight and continuity. Percussion introduces pressure. The synthesizers retain the emotional quality that has long characterized his work. Together, these elements produce music that remains unmistakably his. Islands Alight retains a strong connection with his recent history. Weeds had already demonstrated how detail could become structure and how limited variation could acquire emotional significance. His work with Ian Hawgood confirmed his ability to treat sonic material with extreme patience. The new record introduces a different kind of mobility. The writing appears more sensitive to weight, entrusting rhythm with a greater share of the tension. The environmental theme identified by the artist also enters into this perspective. Murray has linked the record to heatwaves, drought, and a form of ecological anxiety connected to the present. These references operate as an internal pressure within the project. The titles evoke waters, islands, calms, marine animals, and currents. They provide essential coordinates while keeping meaning open. The music proceeds according to its own logic, allowing those images to operate at a deeper level. Murray builds tension using limited means :: The cover follows the same sense of restraint. The original photograph is transformed until color, material, and folds become its dominant features. With only a few elements, the image suggests change and fragility. Its connection with the record is immediate precisely because of its sobriety. The most interesting quality of this album lies in the way Murray manages continuity. Duration makes minute transformations perceptible. The music demands concentration, yet soon reveals a very clear internal scale. A detail that initially seems marginal can acquire prominence several minutes later. A pulse can change its function through a simple shift in context. In this way, Murray builds tension using limited means. Melody retains a decisive role. The harmonies possess the controlled melancholy already present in his previous work, but here they are exposed differently to rhythm, bass, and effects. The production follows the same principle. Definition is high, the detail carefully handled, and depth meticulously managed. The technical work maintains an evident musical function. Murray uses control to give the individual elements autonomy and to make small differences in weight and intensity perceptible. Even in the densest passages, the sound remains clear and readable. Such rigorous control also entails an element of risk. Some passages display a highly regulated timbral continuity, leaving less room for the unexpected. Yet this choice is entirely consistent with the character of a record that demands time and a willingness to engage with slowness. Its idea of movement develops through persistence and internal variation. Some listeners may find this discipline severe. It is also the point at which James Murray expresses his concept of composition most clearly. Trust in the listener therefore becomes central. The record offers few explicit signals and allows meaning to emerge through duration. Some elements gain importance when they disappear. Others appear almost motionless, yet change their function through a new rhythmic relationship. Complexity presents itself with great discretion. Complexity presents itself with great discretion :: This makes Islands Alight a significant work within Murray’s discography. It brings together melodic sensitivity, an interest in electroacoustic material, precision in sound design, and a rhythmic investigation developed with particular depth. The influence of dub history expands the tools at his disposal and shapes his treatment of space, pulse, and the studio. The ambient dimension continues to inform his sensibility, in keeping with the open and undogmatic definition Murray himself has always preferred for his music. The result possesses a particular strength because it avoids the need to announce its change. Islands Alight works as an internal development. Elements that have long been present find a different proportion and produce new consequences. Murray knows his own language well and modifies its rules with precision. The title itself contributes to this impression: two words containing ideas of light, heat, exposure, and a mental geography reduced to a few signs. The environmental anxiety identified by the artist adds another layer of tension. Murray allows it to operate beneath the surface of the work. The beauty of the record often arises from this caution, from its ability to suggest a problem through form rather than turning it into a declaration. Islands Alight works as an internal development. Elements that have long been present find a different proportion and produce new consequences. Murray knows his own language well and modifies its rules with precision. ~Mirco Salvadori After repeated listening, the maturity of the project becomes clear: this is the work of a musician deepening his own vocabulary and changing the way it behaves. The rhythmic component opens new possibilities, the attention to detail preserves its coherence, and the emotional dimension finds a more physical balance. Islands Alight seems to define a precise phase in his artistic trajectory. Murray’s poetry emerges from his control of material and his trust in time. A small number of decisions can transform an entire passage. A sound acquires meaning through position, duration, and memory. This precision gives the record an intense yet measured presence. Islands Alight is one of the most accomplished works of James Murray’s recent career. A focused, patient album, capable of expanding his research through rhythm, space, and studio transformation. Murray’s voice remains perfectly recognisable and here finds a new substance. Islands Alight is available on quiet details. items._cn_summary: James Murray 的《Islands Alight》延续了其多年来在电子音乐与电声形式领域的克制美学，将打击乐提升至结构核心，低频获得重量，回声重塑形体，律动改变各声部间的关系。Dub 音乐中的空间感、聆听文化与录音室转化手法被融入个人化的声音研究之中。四年的创作周期带来高度连贯的整体感，作曲家偏好通过声部之间的相互关系让单一元素改变功能——节奏图形经由细微位移获得切入感，和声序列退后使次要细节浮现。控制严谨而几乎不露痕迹，段落被给予充分的时间发展功能，解决被推迟，满足感往往在长时间停留于同一声音场域之后才到来。合成器保留了情感质感，打击乐引入弹性脉搏，使音乐在保持作者一贯辨识度的同时增添了更具身体性的移动维度。

items.body: Simon Heath closes the release notes with “May you rest in peace.” There’s nothing to add to that. The Yasu Ether Project is an overall haunting and pleasant experience, a final document of an artist who understood that darkness and stillness aren’t opposites of beauty but conditions under which a particular kind of beauty becomes possible. César Alexandre knew that instinctively, and this album proves it one last time. A quiet closing chapter The Yasu Ether Project by Mount Shrine   Cryo Chamber has held the bar for exploratory dark ambient music with a cinematic edge since Simon Heath (the artist behind Atrium Carceri) founded the label with a collaborative focus that has become its defining characteristic. The catalog spans deep space drone, horror-influenced soundscapes, Lovecraftian collaborative projects, and the kind of patient, immersive dark ambient that rewards extended, solitary listening. Among its most beloved artists was Mount Shrine—the project of César Alexandre, a Brazilian producer from Rio de Janeiro who grew up absorbing Brian Eno, Burial, Aphex Twin, and Akira Yamaoka‘s score for Silent Hill 2 before finding his own voice in lo-fi field recordings, vinyl crackle, tape hiss, and long meditative drone structures. He debuted on Cryo Chamber with Winter Restlessness in 2018, followed by Ghosts on Broken Pavements in 2019. He also worked under Mount Hibiki and released vaporwave under the name Lindsheaven Virtual Plaza, an early and influential figure in that scene. César Alexandre passed away on April 15, 2021, from COVID-19. He was one of the first artists whose work made people fall in love with ambient music, and the void he left has been felt consistently in the years since. Cryo Chamber has honored his memory carefully—releasing All Roads Lead Home in 2022 and The Mount Hibiki Tapes in 2024, and The Yasu Ether Project arrives now as the final piece of audio he ever sent to Simon Heath. A version had previously appeared on his own Bandcamp before the page closed. Now preserved and released once more, it stands as a quiet closing chapter. There is a somber feeling that comes with reading about this release before you press play, and that feeling doesn’t leave once you do. Listening to this is the last remnant of his feelings and emotions, the final transmission from an artist whose music offered rest, solitude, and quiet escape to everyone who found it. Just like most Cryo Chamber releases you can expect a very dark and soft ride through the entirety of the album, but there is something that peaks through all the darkness, a simple peace that is haunting. You don’t know what it is that’s calming about it. Maybe it’s the field recordings of birds and daytime, the remembrance of what it feels like when you’ve just woken from a bad storm. Unsettling and peaceful at the same time. That’s how it feels listening to this. Unsettling and peaceful at the same time :: “Gaseous Peak” and “Polysunset” are the standouts on this release. The entirety of the album is wrapped in vinyl hiss, that persistent crackle that was always central to Mount Shrine‘s identity, the sound of something being played back from a medium that’s been worn down by time. It gives the record a physical texture, a sense that these recordings exist in a material world even as the music itself drifts away from one. The closing track is something different. The synths here aren’t just simple pads and atmospheric textures like the rest of the album. Little vocal touches, small nothings, barely registered, appear as the pads build. A small key arp plays in and out, and the visual being created in your head as you listen is genuinely peaceful in a way that feels earned after everything that preceded it. The contradiction at the heart of this closing track is what makes it so affecting, the familiar Mount Shrine darkness is still present, but something lighter has been let in, a crack of warmth that sits differently knowing what this release represents. Simon Heath closes the release notes with “May you rest in peace.” There’s nothing to add to that. The Yasu Ether Project is an overall haunting and pleasant experience, a final document of an artist who understood that darkness and stillness aren’t opposites of beauty but conditions under which a particular kind of beauty becomes possible. César Alexandre knew that instinctively, and this album proves it one last time. The Yasu Ether Project is available on Cryo Chamber. items._cn_summary: 这是巴西制作人César Alexandre（Mount Shrine）于2021年因新冠去世后，由Cryo Chamber厂牌发行的最后一部遗作。专辑延续了他标志性的田野录音、黑胶底噪与磁带嘶声元素，融入漫长的冥想式嗡鸣结构，营造出既不安又宁静的听觉体验。评论指出，黑暗与静默在此并非美的反面，而是某种独特美感得以显现的条件。专辑从夜鸟鸣叫、雨后沉寂等田野采样出发，将环境声与深沉的低频铺垫结合，使聆听过程成为一次缓慢渗透的情绪旅程。作为艺术家最后的情感与声音遗存，这部作品承载着告别意味，同时延续了Cryo Chamber厂牌在电影化暗氛围领域的一贯探索。

items.body: Durable Oxide announces itself with DOX-001—the debut release from a new Portland, Oregon-based label intent on delivering decisive electronic atmospheres. It’s a strong opening statement for a label to make, and Radio Free Money earns it. Textured electronic music with an edge of menace Radio Free Money by Latest Fad   Durable Oxide announces itself with DOX-001—the debut release from a new Portland, Oregon-based label intent on delivering decisive electronic atmospheres. It’s a strong opening statement for a label to make, and Radio Free Money earns it. For a first release, the RIYL speaks volumes: Demdike Stare, Stars of the Lid, The Heartwood Institute, Castles In Space. That’s a specific compass pointing toward slow-burn, cinematic, deeply textured electronic music with an edge of menace, and Latest Fad delivers exactly that. Latest Fad is a duo—Paul Uusitalo and Dan Wilk, members based in Portland, OR and Seattle, WA, who have been collaborating on professional video software together for decades before turning their full attention to music in earnest in 2019. Their previous two albums came out on their own imprint Fading Systems. Radio Free Money is the​ir third full-length and their first on an outside label, employing banks of antiquated synthesizers, modern workstations, analog effects devices, and stringed instruments woven into an electroacoustic pastiche of submerged melodies, hidden rhythms, drops that never arrive, and hopeful/mournful atmospherics. The description “both claustrophobic and infinitely expansive” is apt—this is music that feels like it’s pressing in and opening outward at the same time. Simple ambience, but it works :: At first, Latest Fad is genuinely mysterious—you don’t know what to expect when you press play. This leans toward the ambient experimental side of things but has melodic aspects woven through. “Business Hugs II” arrives as the second track and introduces a static stutter effect that’s immediately intriguing, it opens a conversation the rest of the album keeps having with itself. This plays more as a collective than a conventional album, tracks functioning as interconnected environments rather than separate songs. “Overgrowth Mindset” is one of the most melodic pieces on the release—keys, off-rhythmic tones, and a bassline that brings some light into what is otherwise a consistently dark listening experience. Simple ambience, but it works as contrast against the heavier material surrounding it. “Aberrant Tool & Die” is another interesting piece—its only rhythm is a stable boom with a building single-note cymbal hit, that stale one-note repetition becoming hypnotic as other sounds and effects surface in the background before the track ends in a very dark place. Restraint is the operative word here. The track knows what not to do, and that’s half the work. “Live Laugh Loop” is the favorite of the release—a sad, dark melody with a flanged note sweeping in that makes the intro deliberately hard to parse. The distortion on the pads creates a density that almost obscures the other elements underneath, but those elements are there and they emerge gradually. Nothing here follows a conventional melodic pattern. The only thing obeying musical note rules is the distorted pads themselves—everything surrounding it is off-tone, and that off-tone quality is exactly what gives the track its dark, closing character. As a final statement it lands well. For a label’s debut release, Durable Oxide has set a clear and credible tone. Labels like Castles In Space and The Heartwood Institute built their identities one carefully chosen release at a time, letting the catalog define the aesthetic rather than announcing it upfront. DOX-001 suggests Durable Oxide understands that logic. Radio Free Money is a strong opening argument for what the label intends to be. Radio Free Money is available on Durable Oxide. items._cn_summary: Latest Fad 由 Paul Uusitalo 和 Dan Wilk 组成，两人合作开发视频软件多年后于2019年转向音乐创作。《Radio Free Money》是他们的第三张全长专辑，也是首张由外部厂牌 Durable Oxide 发行的作品。二人使用大量老式合成器、现代工作站、模拟效果器与弦乐乐器，编织出电声拼贴风格的作品，呈现沉没式的旋律、隐蔽的节奏、永不到达的坠落段落以及希望与哀悼交织的氛围。专辑被描述为既具幽闭感又无限开阔，音乐仿佛同时向内挤压又向外延展。整体偏向环境实验领域，同时具备旋律性，各曲目更像是相互关联的空间环境而非独立歌曲，乐评特别提到《Business Hugs II》的静态卡顿效果、《Overgrowth Mindset》的旋律光辉以及《Aberrant Tool & Die》以一记稳定低音与单音钹声构建的催眠式节制手法。

items.body: Presumed finished after the death of founding member Richard H. Kirk, Cabaret Voltaire have instead returned to the stage with a vengeance, selling out shows, resurrecting old collaborations, and proving that their dark industrial pulse still hits hard in 2026. We caught up with Stephen Mallinder to talk about the reunion, the tour, Richard Kirk, and bringing the Cabs’ music back to life. Cabaret Voltaire rise from ashes But What Time Is It Really? by Cabaret Voltaire CODE (2026 Remastered Digital Deluxe Edition) by Cabaret Voltaire   For a group missing a founding member and presumed kaput for good after his death, Cabaret Voltaire have been busy. But 2026 has been a year of surprises and unexpected reunions. Among them, Cabaret Voltaire shines, with sold-out shows across Europe and the United States. Stephen Mallinder, one of the founding members, hit the stage with Chris Watson, who left the group in the 1980s, for an incredible tour of Europe. Now, Cabaret Voltaire returns to the States as they herald the re-release of CODE, their 1987 industrial dance masterpiece. “It’s been amazing to see the world again on tour,” said Mal as he prepared for their first show in the States on this last leg of their US tour. “The crowds ​are a great mix of people, with fans going way back as well as new fans. It’s been great to see younger folks at the shows really getting into it. Nice to see Cabaret Voltaire continues to bring people out.” Folks who want to hear how the band sounds after all this time can check out But What Time Is It Really?, a live recording from Cabaret Voltaire’s shows in the UK, including Sheffield, where it all began. Mal and company bring the classics to the stage with a new life and vitality. The songs sound very much like live versions fans will know, but with an updated edge that doesn’t rehash the material so much as enliven it, reminding us why their music became popular worldwide and remains so to this day. The themes and lyrics remain harshly relevant and resonant at a time when fascism isn’t being left behind closed doors anymore. “It was a concern when we were coming over to tour the West Coast,” said Mal when asked about visiting the States during a time of authoritarian crackdown. “We didn’t know what to expect. But it’s been okay and nothing out of sorts, really. No hassle playing—nothing like the old days when Mussolini Headkick came out and we had Nazi skinheads showing up to gigs! Those were rough, but we wanted to provoke people, to bring out a reaction, which we certainly did. But we’re not playing out-of-the-way places where people may not know our music. We’ve always played cities like New York, Chicago, or San Francisco, where we have a lot of longtime fans. But in San Francisco, for instance, there was a larger number of trans and gay kids at the show, which was great to see. People coming out to enjoy themselves and express themselves is always good for music and for us. Someone in Poland actually came to a gig dressed as the Microphonies cover, which was a first!”   Louder than ever :: On this leg of the tour, Mal is joined by Benge, a frequent collaborator with Mal among many others; longtime Cabs live member Eric Random; and Tara Busch, who takes over for Chris Watson, who will remain in the UK. “It’s been great playing with Chris again, as well as the rest of the band,” said Mal. “Chris and I are old friends, and we’ve played and toured together a lot. Nowadays it’s more or less the same, except his jokes are more shit than ever (laughs). But seriously, working with Chris and his massive collection of recordings has been incredible. It was interesting for him to learn songs that came after his time, not just ‘Landslide’ and ‘Nag Nag Nag.’ Since there were no stems to work from, Benge and I had to find all the samples with help from Chris.” “Since Chris is sitting out the US tour, Tara Busch has come onboard. Tara is a veteran, so having her come on was a no-brainer, as she’s toured with her band I Speak Machine and has worked with John Foxx and Benge as well,” said Mal. “She works the samples that Chris would, as well as handling other duties. I’ve played with Benge a lot, and Eric has been on The Crackdown and Microphonies as well as on tour with us. It’s a band of old friends.” With such longevity as the Cabs have had, it would be impossible to overlook the absence of Richard H. Kirk, who for several years after Mal’s departure kept use of the band name. As a founding member and one half of the band during their duo era, his absence from the tour is a sad one for fans and the band alike. “No, I don’t think so, sadly,” said Mal when asked if this tour would have been possible when Kirk was alive. “Richard wouldn’t have been interested in doing it with me. Though he did a few shows under the name, it was mostly his own work, from the later albums like Plasticity and International Language. He had an idea that Cabaret Voltaire could be an evolving, changing thing, but then he passed. And one of the things Chris and I wanted to do was not overlook him, but celebrate his part in the music of Cabaret Voltaire. It’s why we start the show with a dedication to him.” Cabaret Voltaire still make noise :: Having rehearsed and then toured the songs for almost a year, are there any plans to release material as the new Cabaret Voltaire? Mal isn’t circumspect. “It’s not like a novelty act or some rehashing of the old hits. In reworking the songs for the tour, we’ve made them so we can play them and have them recognizable, but they’re also new in a way, too. We’ve been recording the shows and lots of video from them as well. We will definitely be releasing some live stuff from it and other things.” The US dates coincide with Mute’s release of CODE, Cabaret Voltaire’s 1987 masterpiece and what some people consider the greatest work of their major-label dance days. “Mute did a fantastic job,” said Mal. “There’s so much material from then that we had to go through, with all the various mixes and remixes and demos from back then. CODE was probably our most overtly political record, which is interesting, touring and playing it in these very different but scary political times.”​ 2026 Final tour dates ::Sept 11 – Dallas, TX – Granada Theater^Sept 12 – Austin, TX – LevitationSept 15 – Chicago, IL –  Metro^Sept 16 – Chicago, IL –  Metro^Sept 18 – Toronto, ON –  Phoenix Concert Theatre^Sept 19 – Montreal, QC – Sat^Sept 21 – Boston, MA – The Wilbur^Sept 25 – New York, NY – Knockdown Center^Sept 26 – Philadelphia, PA –  Underground Arts^Oct 7 – Dublin, The AcademyOct 8 – Belfast, LimelightOct 10 – Birmingham, Town Hall*Oct 11 – Liverpool, Arts Club*Oct 13 – Nottingham, Rock City>Oct 14 – Cardiff, The Globe>Oct 15 – Bath, Forum*Oct 17 – Newcastle, Boiler Shop*Oct 18 – Glasgow, Barrowland*Oct 19 – Manchester, Albert Hall*Oct 21 – Bexhill, De La Warr Pavilion*Oct 22  – London, Roundhouse*Oct 25 – Sheffield, Octagon*^ w/ I Speak Machine*w/ Gazelle Twin> w/ Fader But What Time Is It Really? and CODE (2026 Remastered Digital Deluxe Edition) are both available on Mute. But What Time Is It Really? by Cabaret Voltaire CODE (2026 Remastered Digital Deluxe Edition) by Cabaret Voltaire  The post Cabaret Voltaire :: Back In The Noise first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Tundra When I first encountered the wonderful world of AACM, it never occurred to me that any of the composers would be even interested in a bourgeois form as opera. I had, like many listeners, associated the AACM with jazz and improvised musics. Well, I was wrong. AACM was formed to insert African and Black American musics and ideas into the established western classical canon, not to avoid, supplant, or necessarily alter western classical music per se, except to include non-western musical ideas and create new works not dependent on the dominant influence of European cultural hegemony. I had been aware of Anthony Braxton’s forays into theater works and, of course, Anthony Davis is finally getting recognition for his striking operas. But George Lewis, with roots in jazz, extended improvisational techniques, and truly experimental composition here shows us a gentle, entertaining theatrical style that is a heartfelt celebration of the AACM. Afterword is in a way a musical sequel to George Lewis’ essential history of the AACM, “A Power Stronger Than Itself”. Here is a musical retelling of the history of the AACM. It is oral history in song. This fine recording of a live performance is an ideal documentation of this opera. Of course one hopes for more live performance but it is a joy to have this recording stand as definitive, daring the challenge to mount another production, to tell this story again. This is a chamber opera, meaning that it does not require a Wagnerian large romantic orchestra with epic staging and many singers with a huge chorus to boot. Only eight musicians and one conductor, three singers, and a cast of cameos comprise this little very listenable gem.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑收录了George Lewis创作的小型室内歌剧《Afterword》，以音乐叙事方式回溯AACM（黑人音乐家促进协会）的历史。作品延续了Lewis在著作《A Power Stronger Than Itself》中的口述史脉络，将非裔与非洲音乐语汇植入西方古典歌剧传统，而非回避或取代后者。编配精简，仅需八位乐手、一位指挥、三位歌手及若干客串角色即可呈现。音乐语言融合了Lewis在爵士与扩展即兴领域的根基，以温和而富于戏剧性的方式致敬AACM的遗产。作为现场录音的正式版本，它为这部作品留下了权威的音响文献，也向未来的重新搬演发出了邀约。

items.body: Toronto-based duo Kazdoura debuted their single “Taa” on COLORS, taking their Levantine psych-rock to the platform’s bare monochrome stage. for a stripped set putting the song’s guitar and voice fully in view. The track opens on intricate guitar motifs over an ominous chord progression, before a steady drum groove settles underneath. Leen Hamo‘s vocal carries the phrasing of vintage Arabic pop, floating over the arrangement as it tightens through the verses and opens into a chorus built on a hypnotic, ride-cymbal-led rhythm. Hamo, who is Syrian, and Lebanese multi-instrumentalist John Abou Chacra formed Kazdoura in Toronto. The name means “to stroll” in Levantine Arabic, and the JUNO Award-winning duo draw on Arabic maqam melodies while layering in psychedelic soul, jazz and funk. The lyrics deal with memory and the difficulty of letting go. The COLORS premiere opens a European run that starts at Spillestedet Stengade in Copenhagen on August 28 and the Habibi Funk Festival in London on August 29 and 30. From there the duo plays the Jam Jar in Bristol on September 3, Norwich Arts Centre on September 4, Peggy’s Skylight in Nottingham on September 6, and a show in Istanbul on September 11, before Paradiso in Amsterdam on September 15 and the Reeperbahn Festival in Hamburg on September 17 and 18. items.body:
Since everyone else has written something about the centennials of Miles Davis and John Coltrane, why not join the parade? It is a good opportunity to look at the timeline of bassists the legendary trumpeter and saxophonist used. Born just under four months apart, the pair worked together under the elder Davis’ name periodically between Fall 1955 and Spring 1957 before a more steady affiliation in 1958-1960.

It is in that latter period that this analysis will begin, as it gives a convenient bit of serendipity: the fact that two of the their most famed albums were made in that period, Davis’ Kind Blue (March 2nd and April 22nd, 1959 for Columbia) and Coltrane’s Giant Steps (May 4th–5th and December 2nd, 1959). And the analysis will end with Coltrane’s death in 1967, which came during the tenure of Davis’ “second great quintet” and before his groups swelled and electrified during his fusion period.

As such, we begin with the same man, the bassist on both those albums: Paul Chambers. He had taken up the bass a decade earlier in his adopted home of Detroit (where he was a student at the seminal Cass Technical High School ... more on that later). He arrived in New York in 1954 at 19. By the time of Kind of Blue and Giant Steps, he had been on over 100 sessions from dozens of leaders, with multiple dates under Davis (with whom he had started working in late 1955) and Coltrane (who had used him for several albums in 1957-58 as well as both fellow sideman for many others and Chambers also hiring Coltrane for his own sessions). In addition to the five albums he led, Chambers played on sessions for Benny Golson, Curtis Fuller, J.J. Johnson, Lee Morgan, Red Garland, Sonny Clark, and Sonny Rollins.

The collaboration between Davis and Chambers was remarkably fruitful before and after Kind of Blue and solidified a part of Davis’ music that had previously seen widely differing players like Tommy Potter, Oscar Pettiford, Al McKibbon, and Percy Heath. The rest of 1959 saw multiple engagements around the country and closed with recordings that would be part of another monumental record, Sketches of Spain, that paired Davis’ group with the Gil Evans Orchestra. 1960 continued that momentum with more Sketches of Spain recording and almost non-stop touring, including two stretches in Europe, from Spring onward. 1961 and 1962 had more of the same activity, the documents being Someday My Prince Will Come and Quiet Nights. Then, quite suddenly, Chambers left Davis’ group in early February 1963.

It should be stated that Chambers did not restrict his activities solely to Davis, recording over four dozen albums during the period with, among many others, Jackie McLean, Wynton Kelly, Benny Golson, Hank Mobley, and Curtis Fuller. And after leaving Davis, he worked steadily with an array of leaders through the end of 1968, sadly passing away from tuberculosis caused and/or aggravated by drug abuse at only 33.

Stepping right into the Davis group was another Cass Technical High School alumnus: Ron Carter. Nearly 26, Carter was already prophesying his prolific career, participating in over three dozen albums since 1960, with the likes of Charli Persip, Yusef Lateef, Eric Dolphy, Don Ellis, Coleman Hawkins, Cecil Payne, Jaki Byard, Wes Montgomery, Bobby Timmons, Tadd Dameron, Dizzy Reece, Ken McIntyre, Milt Jackson, Benny Golson and others, plus waxing his leader debut, Where?, for Prestige subsidiary New Jazz in 1961.

It was Carter’s arrival that heralded Davis’ soon-to-be seminal band, though it took until Fall 1964 for its personnel to solidify. With Carter, Davis recorded Seven Steps To Heaven and played the Antibes festival in 1963. What is interesting though is while the “second great quintet” is thought of as a monolith, the bass chair had some upheaval/fluidity, depending on how you look at it. Gary Peacock – already a veteran and likely the only person to work for both Bud Shank and Albert Ayler – took the chair for nearly six weeks in the spring of 1964, Carter returning thereafter through the end of the year. 1965 began auspiciously with the January recording of E.S.P. but then things derailed with a convalescing Davis unable to play. And when he could, in November and December, Carter, a hot commodity, was absent, spelled by Peacock once more, then Reggie Workman, who had come up around the same time as Carter and had already come and gone in the groups of Coltrane. In 1966, Carter would return to the group but only partially, participating in East Coast performances, shows elsewhere having either Richard Davis, Carter’s only real equal in terms of fecundity, or in the Peacock mold of eclecticism, Eddie Gomez, returning permanently in October, just before the album Miles Smiles. 1967 was similar: Carter was on board when not busy elsewhere, Gomez on call, then Albert Stinson for one show (a little over two years before his passing – see Bass Tragedies column in Issue 94) and then another veteran, Buster Williams, for a tour (and playing on one track of the 1981-released compilation album Directions). Carter would fill a fixed point for all of 1967, including the albums Sorcerer and Nefertiti and would continue with Davis through the middle of 1968.

Like Chambers or perhaps even more so, Carter was also on the greater jazz scene during his tenure with Davis. He recorded on sessions led by his fellow Davis bandmates but also by everyone from Bobby Timmons, Charles Lloyd, Donald Byrd and Bobby Hutcherson to Jimmy Smith, Shirley Scott, Eddie Harris, and Stanley Turrentine, to name only a handful. He has, of course, gone on to be likely the most recorded bassist in jazz history.

Paul Chambers’ time under Coltrane was shorter and more intermittent. After Giant Steps he was part of, along with the rest of Davis’ period band, November 1959 recordings that would partly comprise Coltrane Jazz and be brought back 18 months later as one of three individual bassists taking part in the Africa/Brass recordings (though his contribution was only heard on the 1995 complete sessions version).

Also in 1959 was a Birdland engagement for Coltrane where either Ahmed Abdul-Malik or George Tucker, both established and close in age to Coltrane, were on bass.

In 1960 Coltrane hired the slightly younger Steve Davis in what seems to be his first professional engagement. Davis stayed in the band through the end of the year for all its live dates and played on music recorded in October and released piecemeal on My Favorite Things, Coltrane Jazz, Coltrane Plays the Blues, and Coltrane’s Sound. Though Davis lived until 1987, his credits after Coltrane were slight: the Mangione Brothers, Dave Burns, McCoy Tyner, Kenny Dorham, James Moody, Freddie McCoy, and Eddie Jefferson, all made in the ‘60s. One deviation in the year came via Coltrane’s shared date with Don Cherry, The Avant-Garde, where bass was handled by either Charlie Haden or Percy Heath.

1961 was a year in flux, bassist-wise, for Coltrane. He introduced a concept to which he would return later in the decade by using two bassists for an engagement at Chicago’s Sutherland Lounge in March: Raphael Don Garrett and Workman, the former, about six years younger, working with Roland Kirk, Paul Serrano, and Eddie Harris, the latter 11 years younger, sideman for Gigi Gryce, Donald Byrd, Duke Jordan, Richard Williams, and Dave Pike.

Workman would be part of the aforementioned Africa/Brass, as would, separately, another bassist, Art Davis, already with credits under Max Roach, Lee Morgan, Booker Little, Hal Mooney, Ernestine Anderson, Dizzy Gillespie, Leo Wright, Clifford Jordan/Sonny Red, Abbey Lincoln, and Booker Little. But in May they were together for Ole Coltrane and nearly a month at the Village Vanguard in August. Workman would become the fixed bassist for Coltrane through the end of the year for concerts, including a European tour, and a small portion of the Ballads album from the end of the year. An exception was Workman either alternating or alongside Jimmy Garrison for a November stint at the Village Vanguard.

If not for a family health crisis forcing Workman to leave the group at the end of 1961 and return to his native Philadelphia, he likely would have stayed with the band and jazz history been quite different. It should be said that Workman hardly is a footnote, becoming one of the most revered players of his generation. But it was Garrison who became the anchor. Born between Garrett and Workman, prior to joining Coltrane he had worked with Philly Joe Jones, Curtis Fuller, Kenny Dorham, Jackie McLean, JR Montrose, Walter Bishop, Jr., Ornette Coleman, Bill Barron, and Ted Curson.

Unlike Carter and Davis, once Garrison was on board, he stayed there. That was mostly to do with Coltrane’s packed schedule of touring and albums and that, unlike Davis, he was healthy and non-combustible. From 1962-1964, Garrison was omnipresent, including the bulk of Ballads, Duke Ellington & John Coltrane (where he split duties with Ellington’s period bassist Aaron Bell), 2018 discovery Both Directions At Once, John Coltrane And Johnny Hartman, Impressions, Crescent, another new millennium unearthed gem in Blue World, and closing out the year with Coltrane’s magnum opus A Love Supreme (which added Art Davis for a second day of recording, released as a second disc to the album’s deluxe edition in 2002).

In 1965 Garrison was still the main man but occasionally Davis would be alongside him: partially on The John Coltrane Quartet Plays in February and fully for June’s Ascension. Otherwise, Garrison was the sole bassist for performances and most of the other albums: Transition, Sun Ship, and Meditations. The exceptions without Davis were overdubs of Haden for the posthumously released Infinity and Garrett returning to play both bass and clarinet for Live In Seattle (as well as the 2021 archival release A Love Supreme: Live In Seattle), Om, and part of Kulu Se Mama.

1966 was even more Garrison-centric, with the only documented work including a second bassist shows in November and December with Lionel “Sonny” Johnson, the brother of Dewey Johnson, who had played on Ascension. The last year of Coltrane’s life, Garrison was there as well, with one notable absence: the Coltrane/Rashied Ali duet Interstellar Space.

Unlike Chambers or Carter, Garrison was kept so busy during his time with Coltrane that his outside discography at the time is meager, though it does include his sole leader date, Illumination! with the Elvin Jones/Jimmy Garrison Sextet. Otherwise it was sessions with Lorez Alexandria, Coltrane bandmate McCoy Tyner, Sonny Rollins, Bill Dixon, and Robert F. Pozar.

After Coltrane’s death, Garrison kept working but his documentation slowed, his two Blue Note dates with the Jones trio rounded out by Joe Farrell being the most enduring. There were also dates with Rolf and Joachim Kuhn, Clifford Thornton and Nathan Davis, and regular work with Alice Coltrane and Archie Shepp. His final recording came in early 1975 with Beaver Harris and Dave Burrell’s 360 Degree Music Experience. Garrison died of lung cancer in 1976 at 42.
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评以Miles Davis与John Coltrane的百年诞辰为契机，聚焦两人合作期间的重要贝斯手Paul Chambers。文章从1959年《Kind of Blue》与《Giant Steps》的共同参与切入，梳理Chambers在Davis与Coltrane阵营中的大量录音与演出活动，并延伸至他1963年离开Davis乐团后的持续工作与早逝生平。乐评并未直接分析专辑曲目或声响细节，而是通过贝斯手的职业轨迹勾勒出那一代爵士乐手间紧密的协作网络与历史脉络，同时强调Chambers在底特律Cass Technical High School所受的音乐训练及其对多位领袖的支持性角色。整体而言，这是一篇以人物传记视角串联经典爵士时期的回顾性评论，适合了解经典爵士乐背后的乐手生态，但缺乏对具体音乐创作手法的深入剖析。
