items.body:
The previous Ezz-thetics column reflected the near-simultaneous appearance of three works of individual brilliance, solo recordings by Liz Allbee, Hannah Marshall, and John Butcher. In the months since, three mid-size, improvisation-rich ensembles, drawing inspiration from more or less explicit environmental themes have appeared, with varying degrees of composition and improvisation, led by musicians of comparable vision: Magda Mayas, Pascal Niggenkemper, and Marta Warelis.

Each is characterized by different degrees of copyright participation, signalling contrasting relations of composition and improvisation. Magda Mayas’ Filamental’s Murmur, evidently as collective as a murmuration of starlings, is copyrighted in the names of all eight musicians. Pascal Niggenkemper’s d’une rive a l’autre is largely copyrighted to the composer/bassist, 11 of the 17 tracks, with six tracks credited to improvised duets from the eight instrumentalists of the Ensemble Tuvalu. Marta Warelis’s Still Life with Lemons is largely credited to the leader/composer. All recently released, the three come from a specific moment in time, the autumn of 2024: Murmur was recorded in Berlin in September; Still Life with Lemons in Amsterdam in October; d’une rive a l’autre in Berlin in November.

Magda Mayas’ Filamental’s Murmur (Relative Pitch) is an octet with a strong emphasis on strings in its make-up; as well as the leader’s piano, there are two harpists, Zeena Parkins and Rhodri Davies, pretty much covering the terrain of free improvising harpists; two cellists, Aimée Theriot-Ramos and Anthea Caddy; two reeds, alto saxophonist Christine Abdelnour and clarinetist Michael Thieke, and violinist Angharad Davies. Murmur is a singular piece, almost 38 minutes long.

There are few spectacles as emblematic of collective mind as a murmuration of starlings, thousands of birds joined in extraordinary aerobatic maneuvers that mock the reckless waste, noise, and danger of fighter jet ballets. Part of the special genius of Magda Mayas’ Filamental is that it never sounds anything like what one might expect from its string-heavy personnel. Everything is sublimated into quiet percussive events, a music that suggests the sublime piety of chance events in nature, like a light rain on large leaves. Hence, Mayas’ description of the work:

I am fascinated by the coordination and elegance of a flock of birds flying, forming beautiful murmurations, constantly changing, seemingly without effort. This communal act provides protection through the sheer number of birds and their changing position; it is an exchange of information amongst them, and it has a clear collective ending when the flock decides to fly back to the ground.

In Murmur, I want to explore how a large ensemble can make use of these instincts of communal movement, coordination, shape shifting and, eventually, potential simultaneous endings through distinct decisions around material and structure but also shared memories of events that were created together.

The doubling of instruments will lend a certain anonymity to the music, furthered by the frequency of isolated percussive details, whether a sustained note from Abdenour suggests a bowed string instrument, or cellos and/or violin are used for a maze of quarter tones. It’s the very nature of the murmuration that will define this collective composition, hive mind or flock consciousness, yes, some overriding shared awareness, existence, and impulse. With no dedicated percussionist present (depending on how you might classify the piano), this is frequently percussion music of the highest order, struck strings on piano and string instruments create a bevy of string-drum plosives. The collective act itself is essentially harmonious in its nature, the special transparency of string harmonics creating a sonic window that opens onto the Cagean silence of the entire ensemble. The cumulative experience is of an interior soundscape in art channeled through the piano and taking place both in the octet and in the listener. A rare and beautiful sonic act.

Pascal Niggenkemper’s Ensemble Tuvalu’s d’une rive a l’autre (Subran 07) is inspired by Tuvalu, the Polynesian archipelago that is currently set to disappear below the Pacific’s waves in a few decades, a paradisical world doomed by climate change. As with Mayas’ Murmur, the bassist/composer’s ensemble is an octet, made up of instrumental pairings: Ben LaMar Gay’s cornet with Louis Lorain’s trumpet; Mona Matbou Riahi’s clarinet with Joachim Badenhorst’s; Tizia Zimmermann’s accordion with that of Artemis Vavatsika’s; Niggenkemper’s double bass paired, less precisely, with Elisabeth Coudoux’s cello. Each of the musicians will also have a vocal role, singing, chanting, or reciting, and Jaumes Privat will appear near the end of the work for an extended spoken word passage.

In her expansive liner note, Julia Neupert, cites the composer’s overarching concerns here:

Niggenkemper is interested in how differently people are shaped – culturally, socially, emotionally – not only in musical terms. He is concerned with broadening perspectives, recognizing other points of view, and collective thinking and creation. In this way, the project also reflects a central cultural value of Tuvaluan society: “Kaitasi” – the principle of always shaping one’s own life in connection with the community. An idea that could hardly be more relevant in our time.

d’une rive a l’autre is a work of daunting complexity. In a “live” staging, drums and metal discs are center stage; a series of 16 sound curtains of plastic and metal with exciter resonators activated by foot pedals surround the stage. All the musicians sing and speak traditional Tuvaluan songs and poems as well as singing freely adapted poems drawn from multiple languages. It comes as both a CD and a DVD. The CD was recorded over four days in the Südwestrundfunk Baden-Baden studio. It has 17 tracks and represents something like the totality of the audio work. The DVD was recorded with an audience in the Tollhaus Karlsruhe a day later. It has 12 tracks, is significantly shorter, sacrifices the instrumental duets, but is enriched by sheer theatrical intensity. Either way, it’s stellar work, with Niggenkemper’s insistence on a humane art reflecting both human potential and the necessity of engaging our collective condition with work of special power. The multiple demands that he places on his musicians are answered with stunning results in the additional tracks on the studio recordings, reflecting the brief individual duets among the matched instruments.

The DVD performance was also presented on the Free Jazz Blog at the time of its release, and it remains available online. It’s an immediate introduction to the work’s combination of visceral emotional power and often luminous instrumental textures:

https://www.freejazzblog.org/2025/03/pascal-niggenkempers-tuvalu-ensemble.html

Marta Warelis’s Still Life with Lemons (Relative Pitch) may be less immediately shaped by environmental concerns than the preceding, but lyric ideas of landscape and the impress of environment still figure in her compositions, from “Birds” to “The Sky Blushes Sunset” to “Ashes to Sea.” The group is a multi-national sextet, with the Polish pianist/synthesist Warelis joined by Hollander Ab Baars, clarinet, tenor saxophone; Canadian Karen Ng, clarinet, alto saxophone; Norwegian Ingebrigt Håker Flaten, double bass; and Americans Ben LaMar Gay, trumpet and electronics and Frank Rosaly drums and gongs. That might suggest a forceful, wind-driven ensemble, but the emphasis is reflective, intimate, sometimes pensive, often witty. Thin instrumental textures predominate, sometimes with different instruments’ sounds penetrating one another, even creating beat patterns as pitches approach one another.

The opening “Birds” begins with an extended solo piano passage immediately emphasizing a certain intimacy. It will persist as the horns enter, with significant dissonance, in a slow interweaving of instrumental voices, ultimately matching the longing of the winds’ theme against the chaotic rush of Warelis and the rhythm section. “There to the Bridge,” an Albanian folk song, receives a plaintively nostalgic performance with Gay setting the mood before the two clarinetists carry the mournful theme to its furthest reaches. The band possesses genuine wit, as apparent in “Alternate Endings,” continuously propelled by Warelis and Håker Flaten’s broken rhythms, effectively extended by the flaring tone of Gay’s trumpet and the dense squawking supplied by Baars’ tenor saxophone. “Intermittent Web of Sorts” proceeds from the initially hesitant patterns of Håker Flaten and Rosaly before Warelis and Gay introduce the theme, textures gradually accumulating. It ultimately reaches an accumulation of sustained winds and electronics, pitches sliding in and out of beat patterns, a high point in the music’s special interconnectedness.

items.body:
1970 (April 10th, 1970 – IBC Studios, London)

Negotiations were now underway between Sean Murphy and several labels including Deram, CBS and Harvest, the EMI sub-label that had distributed Volume Two in the UK and already had Kevin Ayers in its stable. “They are still not an attraction in the very top bracket, so it was a pleasant surprise to see major companies throwing in genuinely massive bids earlier this year when the group was looking for a recording deal,” Richard Williams revealed. Ultimately, Soft Machine signed with CBS, but Third was self-financed, taken partly from studio sessions, but also from live recordings (“Facelift”) and edits and loops of tapes made by Mike Ratledge and Hugh Hopper at the home of Bob Woolford, who had let them use his Brenell and Stellavox tape recorders. Such infringements of accepted professional practices were only possible because CBS, having acquired a finished album, were no longer in a position to force the band to comply with them.

The benefit for Soft Machine in terms of artistic freedom is easy to measure. But this has to be balanced against the fact that the production on Third is, to put it bluntly, an unmitigated disaster. IBC, at the time the studio of choice for such notorious perfectionists as The Who and the Bee Gees, are probably less to blame than the band themselves who, in spite of the issues with Volume Two, are again credited as sole producers. The sound suffers from almost constantly saturated low frequencies and extremely vague mediums, the drums are much too low in the mix, as if played behind a closed door; and the organ is deprived of much of its biting impact through overwhelming equalization. Unfortunately the 2007 remaster, while an improvement, fails to rectify this.

What is problematic is that, as well as making the album an uncomfortable listen, its sub-par production lessens the claim, widely held at the time of its release, that Third represented musical state-of-the-art. This claim was based on Soft Machine’s ability, unparalleled among their contemporaries, to draw from and amalgamate an exceptionally wide range of influences. Starting out as a rock band, and then gradually moving towards jazz to invent a uniquely personal, and absolutely valid, British answer to American fusion, Soft Machine went even further, incorporating the influence of Stockhausen’s avant-garde and Terry Riley’s repetitive minimalism. Third’s ‘total’ vision, encompassing the entire spectrum of known musical genres, placed Soft Machine at the forefront of musical “progress” in 1970. However, horizons have since expanded to such an extent, beyond the Western tradition in particular, that this concept of universality has aged considerably.

In his insightful review of Third for Actuel, Paul Alessandrini wrote of “music to really listen to, no longer aiming for a purely physical vibration, more interiorized. Soft Machine have re-thought their musical influences – Riley, Cecil Taylor, Coltrane – to really make them their own, abandoning their aesthetics of random explosion in favor of a much more thought-out approach.” There are still occasional reminders of these sonic excesses that, as Alessandrini noted, had now largely disappeared from their music. Mike Ratledge's lengthy solo introduction to “Facelift” almost sounds like an electric exorcism, as if to rid Soft Machine of what still remains of that violence in order to reinvent their music in a more controlled manner, setting formal perfection as their new objective.

Considered as a whole, Hugh Hopper's piece represents the last remnant of Soft Machine’s early days, when they still favored spirit over form - here found lacking in both sound quality and performance, with a few train wrecks along the way - and were intent on disregarding the accepted rules. “Facelift” includes free sections increasingly at odds with Ratledge’s preoccupation with structure – and while as a keyboard player, he still embodies the band’s more radical leanings, Ratledge’s own compositions reveal a much less iconoclastic temperament. Hopper described his own approach at the time as “halfway between” that of Dean, “whose thing is really total improvisation, without any structure, and on the other extreme, [that of Ratledge] who's into entirely formalized musical forms.

“Moon in June” completes Robert Wyatt’s donation to Soft Machine of the material originally intended for his first solo album in 1968. It is interesting to note that Wyatt does this at the exact point where Soft Machine had shed any remaining reference to pop in their live repertoire. Looking back, Wyatt was certainly justified in saying that his side of Third was “the last chance I had to use all the things we'd done without being a jazz band. I wanted to get twenty minutes of it down somewhere.” And since his colleagues, reluctant to act as mere accompanists, had made no secret of their lack of interest in his songs, he recorded most of “Moon in June” on his own, repeating the modus operandi of the 1968-69 demo. Hugh Hopper and Mike Ratledge’s participation is again limited to the organ solo halfway through (Hopper also plays a short melodic theme earlier in the piece). Elton Dean wasn’t asked to contribute anything – Wyatt’s unconvincing justification being that he “hadn’t yet worked out how to work on [his] stuff with the added wind instruments.”

As there was no mention of this breach of band discipline in the sleeve notes, only the most astute listeners noticed that the organ heard during the first ten minutes was a Hammond rather than Ratledge’s signature Lowrey, that the playing clearly wasn’t Ratledge’s, and that most of the ‘bass’ parts were played on an electric piano. When the truth was finally revealed, Wyatt gave contradictory versions of what had happened – in one interview claiming that Ratledge and Hopper had “refused to play [on “Moon in June”] and I had to play it all myself,” in another that he’d “almost had to force them to get them to play on it, which I thought was rather unfair as I’d done my best to get into the music they were writing.” Probably the most objective and believable of Wyatt’s rationales was that he was “terrified it’d be played wrong” if he didn’t perform it all himself.

To approach “Moon in June” as a ‘message’ song would misrepresent Wyatt’s more mundane intent, insofar as the phonetic qualities of the words often seem to matter more to him than their meaning. In other words, “Moon in June” is above all a musical composition, a suite of instrumental sections, some of which are adorned with melodies and lyrics, and others not. The singing accompanies the music rather than vice-versa. In this respect, outside of a possible rivalry with Elton Dean and Wyatt’s inability to sing while drumming, there was no theoretical incompatibility between Soft Machine’s move towards jazz and the continued presence of Wyatt’s voice (even if limited to the Echoplexed scat singing of his solitary interludes during the band’s concerts). Dispensing with vocals was the single most questionable move in Soft Machine’s entire musical evolution, not to mention one whose commercial consequences cannot be underestimated. In different circumstances, Hugh Hopper would surely have joined Wyatt in lobbying for having at least some vocals, but in addition to his increasingly strained personal relationship with Wyatt, Hopper had at this point completely lost interest in non-instrumental music. “I find that using the human voice means asserting limitations to your music right from the start”, he explained in 1972. “I am more interested in the sounds generated by instruments, or electronic devices, because the possibilities offered by songs are much more limited than when experimenting with sounds.”

Even if there was no future for singing in Soft Machine, “Moon in June” at least offers evidence that Robert Wyatt, in a voice-free context, could still be more than “a session drummer for an interesting new species of jazz groups,” as long as he contributed to the writing. When it came to extended pieces, he could stand comparison with Mike Ratledge, even though he lacked any comparable academic background. In addition to its constant melodic inspiration, “Moon in June” is very skillfully constructed (indeed, its instrumental architecture had remained intact since 1968), and confirms Wyatt’s seemingly innate talent for making a coherent whole out of ill-assorted musical ideas.

items.body: Do you believe in ghosts? In his book, Ghosts of My Life: Writings on Depression, Hauntology and Lost Futures, Mark Fisher explored themes of being haunted by futures that failed to happen. Inner monologues contain their own hauntings, but the supernatural kind shouldn’t be ruled out, the supernatural in this instance being an entirely natural phenomenon that goes beyond current scientific understanding or explanation. A spectral presence seems to occupy Without. It either crosses over into the physical world naturally and by its own accord or is called unexpectedly forward via an evening séance, but it’s also the ghost of a past that leaks into the present and refuses to stay buried. Death colours, overshadows, and influences everything in this life, but Andrew Sherwell’s latest ambient record, released through Shimmering Moods Records, seems to suggest that, in the final, concluding seconds, there’s no need to fear; everything is okay, and will be once again. What is there to fear, when angels are there to call one home at the moment of departure? When the eyes go blank and the music stops, when the erosion of the world’s background noise – static, hisses, and crackles – finally ceases, there isn’t anything to do other than for the soul to leave the body and drift into an upward shaft of light. The afterlife is hinted at here, but with music as divine as this, Heaven appears to have already broken through. This isn’t a clichéd chorus or a choir of angelic song, but rather the exhalation of a long-dead monk or a wisp of cooler air in a temperature-controlled room. It’s the sound of footsteps in the same room when there’s no one else around, and the feeling of another being present. A faint melody is sung in the background, but it arrives in stages and swells of reverb, perfuming the room with a tantalising glimpse of something beyond, but trailing off before a definitive answer can be given. Both answer and truth lies in the heart rather than the mind, and Sherwell’s music is of the heart. Something is breaking through, but it happens in a subtle way, which makes it all the more dramatic. Above all, the ambient leaves one feeling light-headed and at peace. Although the music has a spiritual side, it can be easy to entangle oneself in its spirituality. The ambient is thin enough to belong to the air, the kind of ambient that engulfs and enwraps one completely, leaving one comfortable and secure in the shadow of its wings. The music is sparse and still feels complete, but the title of Without speaks of a loss. The song, the ghostly cry, is lost in the air. There’s a painful longing to reach out to someone dear, but the chasm between life and death separates them. In this world, things break and fall apart; things live and die. There are other deaths than the bodily kind, and some are more painful than the inevitable one. Andrew Sherwell processes this with delicacy and a slightly mournful air settles over the sighs, the lower rumblings. But there’s also a great clarity to the music, of finally breathing fresh air after a realisation and a polluted mind set free of worry. This is a taste of Heavenly music. Believers and non-believers can both appreciate music as sensitive and as heart-wrenching as this. Go then, there are other worlds than these. Hearing is the last sense to go. www.shimmeringmoodsrecords.bandcamp.com
items._cn_summary: 这张氛围专辑以极简而绵密的声响构建出一个超验的听觉空间，乐评将其形容为一种幽灵般的存在，游移于生死与过往之间。音乐中隐约的旋律被大量混响包裹，像从远处飘来的歌声，在抵达之前便消散于空气中。背景中的静电、嘶嘶声与爆裂噪音并非杂质，而是构成整体氛围的重要纹理，使作品在空灵之外带有物质性的触感。整体基调宁静而略带哀伤，稀疏的编排却维持着完整的情绪张力，仿佛在寂静中触摸某种不可见的存在。值得聆听之处在于它不依赖强烈变化或戏剧性展开，而是通过细微的声音层次与留白，营造出沉浸式的沉思体验。乐评特别强调其精神性维度，认为音乐传达出一种安详与释然，在失落与告别的主题下最终趋向平静。对于偏好ambient、drone及实验声响的听众而言，这张作品提供了细腻而富有深度的聆听路径。

items.body: Gregg Kowalsky, aka one half of Date Palms with Marielle Jakobsons embarks on his next solo record here: a diligently executed and inspired exercise in the heatwave of pure tone synthesis records since 1950 dhrupad raga hit Laraaji and Ocean Of Sound writer David Toop… Although the music is perfectly considered and nevertheless antecendent of drone construction, something about the exotic, fruity simile-soundscapes produces an ontological foundation for inspiring repeat earworming. It’s as if the state of things when listening can be pierced by a more negative bygone phase, but the music does not allow for that. I find myself transported back to a sticky seventies kosmiche house party. This effect bodes fantastically for the meaning of the music. The technique to play a long hand stroke over the keys, and stretch this, so to fill an entire exothermic state, is spectacularly realised by the context of drone fixation throughout the album. The metre changes and placement on “Maliblue Dream Sequence” is extremely well done for all the elements this contrives in the aspect of octatonic mode. If the album holding your attention for the duration might be the most neutral compliment to make, all the same the stoicness of it is savourable in a fashion of sufferage with attention span. Gregg Kowalsky has produced a commendable work in every respect. Where some writers could be tempted to throw an unnatural spanner in the works, the record flows smoothly from beginning to end with a beautiful ease from a bewitching talent. Highly recommended! www.mexicansummer.com
items._cn_summary: Gregg Kowalsky的这张专辑以纯音合成器为核心，延续了自1950年代以来印度德里帕德拉格与氛围音乐传统中的长音手法，但通过精心编排的持续音与细腻的声场变化，营造出一种酷热、稠密且带有复古未来感的聆听体验。作品在静止与流动之间取得平衡，反复出现的折衷音色与类比声响景观让听众产生类似七十年代德国泡菜摇滚派对的联想。乐曲在节拍转换与调式运用上尤为考究，尤其《Maliblue Dream Sequence》一曲对八声音阶的处理展现了高度的结构控制力。整张专辑在无人机音乐的框架内保持了流畅的叙事感，并未因实验性而显得生硬或断裂，而是以克制而坚定的方式推进，适合专注聆听并值得反复品味。

items.body: The opening track on The Gloom & The Glowing recalls a deep blue Saturday in July, the kind that’s spent doing nothing much at all apart from lounging in the back yard and tuning into the general malaise of the street. The twinkling notes of an ice-cream truck pass by, but one look at the album’s title is enough to dampen those expectant smiles. Something will cool them off, but it won’t be a Twister or a 99 Flake – it’s the cooler, slightly melancholic vibe of Nonconnah’s music, which sinks in deeply and somehow subdues the atmosphere. Initial appearances can be deceiving, because Nonconnah’s new album seems to warp over time. The husband and wife duo were Lost Trail in a past life, but their music together has shifted into a new season. Much of that earlier sound is still intact: those hazy, spectral layers are added to dreamy harmonies that sleepwalk through thickets and brambles, walking in the soft autumn light and then going further beyond. They conjure up a mixed bag of emotions – their music is first and foremost an emotional experience – with both positive and negative battling for overall control. Sadness seeps outwards, manifesting itself in the gritty rolling waves of distortion and the lighter, exceptionally beautiful harmonies. That rough part of the sound will always be there, but it is, to some extent, tamed and controlled. The abrasive distortion doesn’t drown out the fragile harmony, but it does add to the subtle unease, which is evidenced in ‘The Collapsing Bridge’. It’s as delicate and as heartbreaking as a tear sliding down a cheek, spilling from eyes that drown in rain. The notes swirl in reverse on ‘Cassette Tones For Fall’, and its leaves create a swooning, flickering vision of something lingering just beyond the curtain. The drone is soft and tentative – first steps – gauzy in appearance and pretty in its new dress. Field recordings and vocal broadcasts are peppered throughout, appearing just beneath the surface. ‘Lives Past And Lives To Come’ is full of autumnal light. Its silky tones are draped over the music, and they fall, fall, fall, like a million leaves in slow-motion. Things have been lost and things have been damaged, but it’s still here. This whirling dance carries with it a message of undying romance and tentative hope for its coming years, and both offer protection against the gathering gloom and the growing malignancy of the darkness that stares in through the window. The Gloom & The Glowing by Nonconnah www.nonconnahordeath.bandcamp.com
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以朦胧的音层与梦幻和声构建出独特的情绪空间，失真与优美旋律相互交织，外露的噪音被收束在可控范围内，形成一种沉静却不安的氛围。开篇曲让人联想到慵懒夏日午后，但标题又暗示着更深层的忧郁。田野录音与零散的人声片段隐现于声响底层，为作品增添了私密感。歌曲如《The Collapsing Bridge》以轻柔碎裂的方式呈现脆弱，《Cassette Tones For Fall》通过反转音符与纤细长音制造飘忽的视觉意象，而《Lives Past And Lives To Come》则铺陈出秋日般的光晕，缓慢坠落中带着浪漫与微弱的希望。作为前身 Lost Trail 的延续，创作在保持旧有气质的同时进入了新的季节，整体上是一张情感丰富、层次精密的环境声响作品。

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑延续了乐队对挪威民间旋律的再发掘，但不再依赖科幻合成器的整体氛围，而是回到更贴近地面的音色织体。开场曲以挪威西部的一种跳跃舞曲为基础，萨克斯先奏出旋律，低音提琴与鼓提供节奏支撑，随后叠加模块合成器和颤音琴的音色。乐队成员的分工并不固定，低音提琴后来与萨克斯同度奏出旋律，鼓的节奏也随之敞开，整体转向更自由的即兴状态。其令人关注之处在于民谣素材并未被单纯还原，而是通过灵活的乐器角色、即兴段落和电子音色晕染，使传统舞曲获得新的伸缩空间。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由两位挪威音乐人与一位瑞典音乐家合作完成，素材来自三人的民族传统曲调，但诠释方式远非传统。演奏质感更接近室内乐，三位乐手像在亲密交谈，节奏被打散、重组，甚至中途戛然而止，展现出北欧民间舞曲表层之下阴暗而神秘的气息。开篇曲取自挪威塞特斯达尔山谷的提琴曲，其灵感来自传说中瀑布里教人拉琴的水精灵，小提琴也因此曾被当作魔鬼的乐器。对瑞典波尔卡舞曲的处理同样碎片化，竖笛反复引子后，小提琴引出旋律再齐奏，随即整个声音结构瓦解。专辑在传统与实验之间寻找张力，呈现了一种独特的民间音乐视角。

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以街头录音为基底，记录了芝加哥南区枪击暴力亲历者的口述与即兴说唱。制作人Ian Brennan未添加任何音乐，仅保留环境原声，包括飞机起降、街区噪音与蚊虫声，形成一种未经修饰的声音档案。参与者年龄跨度从17岁到67岁，许多人刚参加完悼念活动，或正在前往悼念的路上，讲述内容涉及失去亲人、社区创伤与生存状态。录音地点位于一位参与者94岁祖母的门廊前，恰逢国民警卫队被部署至芝加哥的当天，背景声与话语内容共同构成强烈的时代语境。作品不是传统意义上的音乐，而是将现实声响直接转化为表达媒介，以近乎纪实的方式呈现个体记忆与社会暴力之间的张力。其艺术价值在于以声音为载体，让边缘群体的叙述获得直接传播的通道，而非通过旋律或编曲进行中介。项目收益将捐赠给致力于以公共卫生方式终结暴力的Cure Violence Global组织，使作品在艺术之外兼具社会行动意义。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — As soon as you start listening to Quickly Quickly Quickly, and their opening track, "Firebears", you are plunged into a sonic explosion you weren't prepared for; it is a surprise that stirs you in much the same way hearing classic 70s bands for the first time did. I was reminded of King Crimson, there is something epic about it, yet also dark and dangerous, and yet I also thought of Sonic Youth, who, incidentally, also feature two guitarists, a crucial element in creating that sonic canvas.The way the keyboards and guitars intertwine was also innovative, and that was nothing compared to what followed, as the McGowan brothers sing with such deep emotion and grit. This sets them apart from other bands that might be solid instrumentally but, at least to my ears, lack a distinctive signature. The arrangements constantly shift and adapt to the unfolding music, a progression that is hard to predict, with the vocals guiding the instruments as they collectively build the melody, reversing the usual dynamic.Contrasts emerge quickly; a more introspective section takes on a nearly jazzy feel, albeit indirectly, and the piano can be as laid-back as Neil Young during the moments when Crazy Horse was resting. Towards the end, at times I thought I heard the voice of Chris Cornell from Soundgarden, specifically during his band's psychedelic moments, and I found that same powerful vocal range, imbued with genuine emotion, once again in The Tea Club."The Eternal German Infant" presents a contrast between its instrumental power, a kind of restrained violence, and the vulnerability of the vocals; it then plunges into imagery woven from seemingly disjointed guitar, bass, and keyboard notes, with the guitar tearing at notes as if seeking a meeting point between the spirit of the voice and the music, a near-theatrical encounter."Mister Freeze" opens another door within the established framework, that dreamlike (or perhaps nightmarish) atmosphere, as if hundreds of crystal shards were parting to clear the way: an acoustic guitar paired with electric strumming that hangs like a curtain of stained glass catching the sunlight. The same notes repeat, yet with a certain decomposition, like fruit left too long in the summer sun. The subtlety of David Sylvian's solo work gains ground, casting a protective mantle, that sheltering sky spoken of by writer Paul Bowles, evoking a desert soundtrack: the organ, the strumming guitar... and one mask concealing another."I Shall Consume Everything" layers on intensity, steadily building tension; drums and a guitar join the keyboards, shifting from the style of the early Fripp (circa 1969) to the Greek echoes of Aphrodite's Child, until a guitar riff finally tears down what was built, driven by distortion, overlapping and repeating vocals, and rhythmic breaks that shatter the melody, causing it to quickly fade away......was any disintegration worthy of the name ever slow?

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以密集的乐器层叠和不断变形的编曲结构为核心，开篇即以爆炸性音墙冲击听众耳朵。键盘与双吉他的交织构成核心织体，McGowan兄弟的演唱在情感张力与粗粝质感之间游走，引导器乐走向而非被动跟随，这在传统前卫摇滚中颇为罕见。专辑在力量与脆弱之间持续切换：内省段落带出隐约爵士气质，钢琴段落松弛如民谣休憩，嘶吼段落则撕裂旋律框架。后期曲目逐步走向解构，重复与失真叠加，节奏断裂使旋律在高潮处骤然消散。整体呈现出破坏性的戏剧叙事，自成一格的器乐对话与声乐张力是其最突出的辨识度。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — One might associate Chile with the folk songs of V�ctor Jara, the psychedelic and progressive past of Los Jaivas, or high-quality pop-rock bands like La Ley; yet Cherc�n offers a pleasant surprise with a bold, distinctive rock sound that draws from psychedelia while incorporating a jazz-infused saxophone and string arrangements, featuring violin and cello, that add nuance to the quintet's (and its guests') fast-paced progressive rock style."La culpa" is the opening track, reminiscent of The Mars Volta in its wild, defiant nature, where the sound builds toward a final climax, intensifying as if funneling through the guitar; the audio distorts while Mart�n Pe�a, the vocalist, belts out vocals that are at once melodic and visceral. There are moments of great freedom, reminiscent of jazz scat singing, that shift into free-jazz passages blended with hard rock. This fusion, combined with the vocalist's delivery (which at times resembles a mystical, inverted prayer), reaches a new level of decibel intensity and opens up a new dimension for the saxophone within progressive heavy rock, distinct from the styles of Van der Graaf Generator (a feat that once seemed impossible) or Gong, two major touchstones for the instrument in this genre. Here, the fusion is more contemporary, yet Kalimba still retains melody and harmony, in abundance, while incorporating folk influences drawn from indigenous music.The instrumental sections still sound as improvised and fresh as when they must have been composed; when the band kicks into highly intricate, distorted rock, backed by the string section, the music gains added weight without losing any power; quite the opposite. Mart�n Pe�a holds his own as a vocalist, knowing exactly how to function as yet another instrument.Tiempos paralelos can serve as a summary of Cherc�n's musical approach, as the first part involves the saxophone and a sense of restraint, while the second features an uprising led by the guitar and a defiant vocal performance, delivering a solo reminiscent of Annie Haslam channeling Ian Gillan. "Las Mentiras del Muro" opens with a powerful foundation of drums and bass that reminded me of the overflowing energy of Rage Against the Machine, though the comparison stops at the vocals, as Mart�n Pe�a handles both the metal and progressive sections with the same care and precision found in the saxophone notes; the sax, for all its delicacy, sounds no less powerful and truly stands out as a key protagonist of the album."Relato de una obsesi�n", specifically its first part, titled "Quimera", features Eastern percussion and rhythms; the quintet achieves such a profound communion that they seem to act as one, wholly absorbed in the task of capturing their vision for posterity. The second part, "El orate," erupts, unleashing the inevitable, a tidal surge that can no longer be contained. It embodies that Eastern-inspired tensi�n, held taut to the point of infinity, until it finally meets the resistance it had ultimately sought, and that fiery blaze, which was in fact its very reason for being, is consumed.As if the ashes still held light and heat after the fire, the album's final track, "Colores," embodies a mysticism that retains its clarity, refusing to be blinded by its own nature, and one that learns and evolves, promising a future that will harvest the seeds sown in this auspicious debut.

items._cn_summary: 智利乐团Chercún的首张专辑展现出大胆的融合取向，将迷幻摇滚与爵士元素编织在一起。萨克斯的加入是这张专辑的核心特色，它并非Van der Graaf Generator式的复古用法，而是在前卫硬摇滚框架内开辟出更当代的声音空间，与小提琴、大提琴的弦乐编制形成丰富的层次。人声方面，主唱Martín Peña将自由爵士的散拍唱法与金属式的爆发力融合，兼具旋律性与侵略性。作品中还融入了源自智利原住民音乐的民间律动，以及东方打击乐的节奏语汇，使整体呈现出跨文化的杂糅感。器乐段落保留了即兴般的鲜活质地，失真吉他段落因弦乐组的支撑而获得额外的重量而不失力量。整张专辑体现出南美新生代乐团在前卫摇滚领域探索个人语法的努力。

items.album: Tomorrows Letters Puts the Mind on Trial with Noir Synthpop Single “Up Against the Wall”
items.excerpt: The whispers in my mind, the echoes of my past, Judgment in the mirror, a reflection that will last. The mind can build a courtroom from almost nothing. A remembered phrase becomes evidence, an old mistake is summoned as a witness, and conscience takes the prosecutor’s table before crossing the room to pronounce sentence from the bench. items.body: The whispers in my mind, the echoes of my past, Judgment in the mirror, a reflection that will last. The mind can build a courtroom from almost nothing. A remembered phrase becomes evidence, an old mistake is summoned as a witness, and conscience takes the prosecutor’s table before crossing the room to pronounce sentence from the bench. No counsel appears for the defense, no statute of limitations applies, and every hour spent alone provides another opportunity to reopen the case. On Up Against the Wall, Minsk-based artist Tomorrows Letters turns this internal proceeding into a severe and stylish piece of noir synthpop. The solo project of Kiryl Karotki, Tomorrows Letters enters the song already cornered, facing a tribunal in which the accused, prosecutor, and judge occupy the same body. A low, saxophone-like drone opens the recording before giving way to a mechanized groove. Sparse piano notes land beside Karotki’s controlled vocal, lending each phrase the gravity of sworn testimony. His delivery remains cold and composed, yet there is considerable force beneath that restraint, like silk draped across the song’s dread. Trip-hop menace and industrial textures run through the rhythm, meeting the darker electronic pop associated with Depeche Mode’s 1990s and early-2000s records. The clipped construction also carries the severe elegance of 1980s new wave and minimal synth. When the saxophone returns between verses, it winds through organ-like keys and a low electronic buzz, giving the track the character of a neo-noir jazz performance conducted inside a machine. Karotki’s voice completes the setting, transporting the listener into a room filled with stark light, suspended haze, and hard silhouettes. Every word appears carefully measured, as though an answer given too quickly could become further evidence for the prosecution. The lyrics make this psychological trial explicit. Past mistakes supply the testimony, the mirror preserves the verdict, and the heartbeat keeps time for fear. Within the “courtroom of my soul,” the singer bears every role and pays every toll. By the outro, the narrow line between right and wrong has become another instrument of captivity: “I’m a prisoner of my own mind.” “The song describes a state where your own mind acts as both the prosecutor and the judge in a trial that never ends,” Karotki explains. “It’s about being your own worst enemy, trapped in a loop of self-judgment where conscience acts as a punisher rather than a moral guide.” The single release of Up Against the Wall, the first offering from Karotki’s debut LP set for release this autumn. It is accompanied by an exclusive remix from Karotki’s friends in Nürnberg, marking the first of several guest appearances and collaborations planned for the forthcoming album. The song was mixed and mastered by Nürnberg’s sound engineer, Andrei Bobrovka, while its cover artwork was created by Tomorrows Letters. Tomorrows Letters is a project that operates according to a strict hardware-only philosophy, with Karotki using vintage samplers and unconventional songwriting methods to give it a dusty, tactile character. New Romantic and minimal synth-pop influences provide the foundation, though their historical language is put in the service of present-day psychological estrangement. Across his work, Karotki examines isolation, self-judgment, Jungian ideas concerning the hidden self, maladaptive daydreaming, compulsive creation, and the pursuit of victories that prove empty once attained. Listen to Up Against the Wall below: Follow Tomorrows Letters: Instagram Bandcamp Spotify YouTube Apple Music The post “Judgment in the Mirror” — Tomorrows Letters Puts the Mind on Trial with Noir Synthpop Single “Up Against the Wall” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: And so, as summer draws to a close and we enter the ever-popular fall season (which affords us the use of the word “autumnal”, which you fucking bet we’ll be working in wherever possible), we also enter the final third of 2026. Of course, needing to get our Year End coverage done and dusted by mid-December means we’ve got roughly three months left of coverage, and the actual determination of what records we liked the most still to come. As always, suggestions of things we’ve overlooked are always welcome, as are your own picks, feel free to toss ’em in the comments below. But of course, this is all a preamble for our most venerable tradition, ye olde Tracks post. Join us won’t you? Creux Lies Pig, “An American Ideal of Beauty” Raymond Watts sure is a busy guy these days. Aside from a massive tour he’s kicking off across North America, the Pig mastermind is following up this year’s enjoyable Hurt People Hurt with a smattering of follow-up EPs. The first of those, from which the track embedded below is taken, is Dirt Box, featuring four new tracks with accompanying remixes by the likes of Stabbing Westward, Combichrist, Cyanotic and Rabbit Junk. Then we’ve got Merciless coming down the pike, a remix EP with cuts by Clock DVA (!!) and Pitchshifter amongst others. I guess you can’t keep a good hog down. Dirt Box by PIG Creux Lies, “Jubilate” Man, but Sacramento’s Creux Lies are keeping us on our toes. The depth and richness of sophomore LP Goodbye Divine has us waiting on a follow-up with bated breath, but the third original track they’ve released over the past couple of years sounds very distinct from its predecessors. Here, they’re in an easily approachable synth dancefloor mode, but the real sauce is in the slowburn approach Ean Elliot Clevenger takes to the vocals which build across its runtime. Jubilate by Creux Lies UNTER STRØM, “Stumbling” UNTER STRØM is the side-project of Alex from LA’s post-punkers Matte Blvck, and while it is a more down the pipe electronic project than its parent band, it’s a far cry from the defacto sound of modern electro-darkwave. Indeed, while the sound of their material is certainly of a more shadowy cast, you’re getting programming and arrangements that refer to more aboveground sounds in the world of progressive house and melodic techno, splitting the difference between those bright club nights and dark underground dancefloors in fine fashion. Between Forms by UNTER STRØM alarm!systemen, “Burn” Don’t let the apparent compositional simplicity of Belgian newcomers alarm!systemen’s approach to melancholy coldwave on this track fool you; there’s a real consideration of colour and harmony here which makes a virtue of modern gear and technique rather than eschewing it for the sage of nostalgia, while shooting a style familiar to fans of any number of early 80s continental acts with a bright and fresh strain of dreampop. alarm!systemen by alarm!systemen Evil Dust, “Sadistic” Some good n’ gnarly lo-fi business from London body music act Evil Dust, whose new LP I Just Want to Fit In is due shortly on the 11th of September. If’n you like some of the stuff that the whole industrialized techno sound was doing, but wish it was, well, more industrial, this might fit the bill; heavily percussive, lots of sample work, and an unruly groove that never quite settles in where you think it will. I JUST WANT TO FIT IN by EVIL DUST Einhänder Aus Stahl, “4 Meter Punch To The Face (Visitor remix)” Speaking of lo-fi body music, the new maxi EP from Einhänder Aus Stahl, the side project of Micheal of Chrome Corps, offers a slew of minimal tracks which strip throwback techno and EBM to their barest skeleton. Throw in a little bit of left-field synth-funk courtesy of Visitor (you probably don’t need us to ID the samples for you) and you have a twitchy, burpy blast of fun. Mebyon Kernow by Einhänder Aus Stahl The post Tracks: August 31st, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._cn_summary: 本文是2026年8月底的月度单曲推荐合集，涵盖四首不同方向的暗潮及电子音乐作品。PIG的《An American Ideal of Beauty》延续工业EBM路线，Raymond Watts再度展现高产创作力，合作阵容包括Stabbing Westward与Combichrist等工业老牌。Creux Lies的《Jubilate》脱离以往暗潮气质，呈现更易接受的合成器舞曲编排，焦点在于主唱Ean Elliot Clevenger层层递进的演唱处理。UNTER STRØM作为Matte Blvck成员Alex的分支项目，融合渐进浩室与旋律techno的明亮质感与暗潮底色，在两种俱乐部美学之间取得平衡。比利时新晋乐队alarm!systemen以《Burn》回归冷波传统，在简约编曲中注入色彩与和声的精心考量，拒绝纯粹怀旧而拥抱现代音色与技术。整体推荐侧重电子与暗潮交汇的当代独立场景，兼顾老牌工业与新生力量。

items.body: A label and collective that kept going, kept releasing, kept refining a shared aesthetic without compromise or concession to trends. aux4444 pt.1 carries all of that history in its drum patterns and melodic builds, and it sounds better for it. This is what underground electronic music looks like when it’s done with genuine conviction over a sustained period of time. Fusing IDM and nostalgia that also carries significant electro elements aux4444 pt.1 by omni causa   mind​color​music is a Berlin-based label that has been operating quietly and consistently since 2009 (and previously as a party series), building a catalog of braindance, IDM, jungle, and breakbeat electronica across limited hand-stamped physical releases and digital editions. The label’s naming scheme immediately stands out—every release carries the “aux” prefix followed by a number, a system that applies across all artists on the roster and functions as a unified catalog language rather than individual release titles. aux44 is the name of the series—44 stands for the precinct number of the Berlin Neukölln borough. It’s a clean, distinctive approach that signals something about how the label thinks about its output, not as a collection of individual artist statements but as a continuous ongoing archive (connected to their location) of a shared aesthetic community. The numbers aren’t just catalog codes; they’re evidence of continuity, of a project that has been running long enough to reach four-digit entries. Once you notice it, it catches the eye immediately. ​omni causa—the Berlin-based producer at the center of the mindcolormusic collective, has been releasing material on the label since its earliest releases, with collaborations alongside tysk raider (as Omnibusraider), microlith, fah, and foreign sequence building a catalog that sits consistently in braindance and IDM territory without ever leaning i​nto the acid-heavy, distortion-forward side of the genre. This is melodic and beat-driven braind​ance, loops, breaks, and emotional structure rather than squelching 303 work. aux4444 pt.1 collects material recorded between January 2021 and September 2024, a three-year span tha​t gives the release a sense of accumulated thought rather than a single session document. “Its Relative” is the standout, the most ambitious track on the release in terms of rhythm and structure. The drums carry it entirely. Distorted kicks and a percussion loop hitting in detuned rhythm with what sounds like broken ring modulation applied create a genuinely compelling effect. The melodic builds surrounding that rhythmic core are well placed, surfacing and receding without competing for space. “Perspectives,” the track that follows, is a happy braindance-ish piece where the drum rhythms and bassline work together as something genuinely catchy. The pads build in a way that’s consistent across the album but lands particularly well here. It has a structural and melodic familiarity that recalls how Cylob organized composition on Cylobian Sunset (1996), not in sound, nowhere near what Cylob produces aesthetically, but in the way melody is laid out and the builds are sequenced. That compositional logic, that familiar approach to developing a braindance track from its initial statement toward something larger, is recognizable here and executed with real confidence. The drum work throughout is the album’s strongest consistent element. Break samples fused with analog drum sounds and what sounds like custom electronic percussions tampered enough to matter, it’s a good fusion of IDM and nostalgia that also carries significant electro elements throughout. That electro thread connects aux4444 pt.1 to a lineage of melodic, beat-focused IDM that ran through the Toytronic label in the early 2000s, artists like Multiplex‘s adjacent work, Gimmik‘s more accessible moments, and producers like Bochum Welt, whose warmth and melodic intelligence sat somewhere between electro and IDM without fully committing to either. mindcolormusic has been doing this long enough that reaching the 44 mark in its catalog numbering feels less like a milestone and more like evidence of something quietly remarkable: a label and collective that kept going, kept releasing, kept refining a shared aesthetic without compromise or concession to trends. aux4444 pt.1 carries all of that history in its drum patterns and melodic builds, and it sounds better for it. This is what underground electronic music looks like when it’s done with genuine conviction over a sustained period of time. aux4444 pt.1 is available on mindcolormusic. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑来自柏林地下厂牌 mindcolormusic，由核心制作人 omni causa 操刀，收录了2021至2024年间跨越三年的创作素材，呈现出累积式的思考痕迹而非一次性即兴录音。作品聚焦于旋律性与节奏驱动的 braindance，融合 IDM 与 electro 元素，回避了 acid 合成器主导的扭曲美学，转而以 loop、break 与情感结构为核心。整张作品延续了厂牌自2009年以来低调而持续的美学路线，强调连贯性而非碎片化。亮点曲目 'Its Relative' 以失真底鼓与失谐节奏环建立骨架，旋律层在空间中有序进退；'Perspectives' 则展示了鼓线与贝斯的紧密咬合，pad 铺垫恰到好处。整体呈现一种坚持信念、不随趋势妥协的地下电子音乐姿态。

items.body: Six tracks, no wasted motion. ARKADA005 doesn’t revive electro; it plugs it back in, turns the voltage up, and lets the machine speak for itself. Drawing on the foundational grammar of electro Marking a welcome return to the furor of contemporary electronic music, London’s Arkada resurfaces with ARKADA005, a six-track workout from Brussels’ Arsonist Recorder and Sigma_ALgebra. This is electro with the futurist chrome stripped back enough to expose the working parts: rolling bass, snapping breaks, brutal low-end pressure and melodies that still know how to carry a tune. The record feels contemporary without straining to prove it, drawing on the foundational grammar of electro while treating that grammar as ​something alive, flexible and available for further damage. Arsonist Recorder takes the first three cuts straight to the machine soul. The rhythms are tight but never sterile, with heavyweight bass movement and synth lines that bring a real sense of propulsion. There is funk here, but it is not nostalgia-funk. It is the physical intelligence of the form: music built to make the body respond while the circuitry does something stranger underneath. Sigma_ALgebra with three tracks that feel like an autopsy performed at club volume. The components are stripped down, isolated and rebuilt into lean, muscular constructions where breaks, bass and synthetic detail lock together with increasingly brutal efficiency. What makes the record work is the tension between its opposing instincts—sweet melody and hard mechanics, precision and abrasion, body-popping unity and 4am chicanery. Six tracks, no wasted motion. ARKADA005 doesn’t revive electro; it plugs it back in, turns the voltage up, and lets the machine speak for itself. Arkada #005 is available on Arkada. items._cn_summary: Arkada厂牌第五期分辑收录了布鲁塞尔两位电子音乐人Arsonist Recorder与Sigma_ALgebra各三首作品。整张专辑延续electro的底层语法，重型贝斯线条与锐利碎拍构成主要驱动力，合成器旋律在机械化框架中保留可辨识的曲调感。前三首由Arsonist Recorder呈现，节奏紧凑但不枯燥，强调律动与机器质感之间的平衡，带有funk的体感却不依赖怀旧情绪。后三首来自Sigma_ALgebra，编曲更趋精简与解剖式，部件被逐一剥离后重组为骨骼分明的结构，碎拍、低频与合成器细节以递增的强度咬合。整张专辑在甜美旋律与硬质机械、精准与粗粝之间维持张力，六首曲目各自独立却共享同一种冷峻的俱乐部逻辑。Arkada作为伦敦独立厂牌延续了对当代电子音乐尖锐面向的关注。

items.excerpt: From Helsinki’s Toinen kerros comes Isthmus Recordings, a new label and live archive capturing the restless, intimate sounds of Finland’s experimental music scene.   Bringing Helsinki’s Sounds Together Kesän korvalla by Koho / Koskenlahti Ballad Broadcast / Lineaments by Isthmus Recordings   Isthmus Recordings is a new record label based in Helsinki and Venice, also functioning as an archive for performances recorded in Toinen kerros, a new community-driven space for practicing and enc
items.body: From Helsinki’s Toinen kerros comes Isthmus Recordings, a new label and live archive capturing the restless, intimate sounds of Finland’s experimental music scene.   Bringing Helsinki’s Sounds Together Kesän korvalla by Koho / Koskenlahti Ballad Broadcast / Lineaments by Isthmus Recordings   Isthmus Recordings is a new record label based in Helsinki and Venice, also functioning as an archive for performances recorded in Toinen kerros, a new community-driven space for practicing and encountering sonic arts which which (in a few phases), has become a hub for the Finnish experimental music scene. The first two releases by Isthmus (directly funding the space with Bandcamp sales) include performances in genres such as electroacoustic improvisation, ambient, and minimalism. Recorded in May 2025 and fittingly titled Kesän korvalla—“on the verge of summer,” but also “with the ear of summer”—the first Isthmus release is a performance by the duo composed of sound artist J. Koho (whose brilliant designs grace the Isthmus cover arts so far) and percussionist Minna Koskenlahti. During the 35-minute piece, Koho / Koskenlahti improvise with amplified and processed concrète sounds, but also with sounds recalling more standard mallet percussion instruments and, later in the piece, wooden flutes and whistles. The improvised piece is organized in movements, with different moods and textures following one another: first frantic but gentle percussions set the atmosp​here, a drone-oriented phase follows and then vitalistic and almost free-jazz wind instruments loudly pierced the tapestry of drones. After this climax, the piece descends back into percussive territory, increasing in intensity and chaos and then falling back into order with long stretches of metallic sounds finally slowing down into ambiance. There is something meteorological about the piece, coming, growing and going like a weather event—a rush of wind moving natural and human objects before a summer shower, and then going and fading in the distance just as it came. Isthmus documents music in motion :: The second Isthmus release (Ballad Broadcast / Lineaments) so far includes two pieces, respectively a duo performance by Mark Reid Bulatović and Simone Spampinato, and a solo piece in two parts by Fredrik Rasten. The whole release focuses on guitars, and particularly acoustic guitars with uncommon tuning, interacting with ambience rather than effects or found sounds. At the beginning of Bulatović and Spampinato’s piece, “Ballad Broadcast,” the recording lets through room noise—a door opening, people moving, camera shutters—which, while most likely just accidental to the composition, add to the quiet and enigmatic guitar arpeggios. Over twenty minutes, the guitars form a very sparse call and response of sorts between a drier and more plucked sound and a strummed one with softer decay, but while they are in dialogue, they don’t offer an obvious interpretation, and the slice around them takes most of the sonic and semantic space. Fredrik Rasten’s piece, “Lineament” is a performance of the 2023 studio album of the same name. The pieces feature guitar arpeggios as the undisputed protagonists, but also held-note vocals and sine drones adding to the texture and interacting with the guitars’ own resonance and vibrations. While part I chooses simple arpeggios overlapping in their upward and downward trajectories as its main shape, in part two chords also enter the equation, giving a less regular effect and more space to the voice and drone. With forthcoming (and past) events at Toinen kerros including fantastic names both from the Finnish scene and internationally, one should really be looking forward to the live performance series growing—and hopefully more outside of the live archive too. (And if you’re in the Helsinki area, make sure to keep an eye on their programming!) Kesän korvalla and Ballad Broadcast / Lineaments are both available on Isthmus. items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评介绍了赫尔辛基新晋厂牌Isthmus Recordings的前两张发行，均为现场录音档案式作品，收益用于支持社区实验音乐空间。第一张收录声音艺术家J. Koho与打击乐手Minna Koskenlahti的35分钟即兴演出，使用放大处理的具象声音、马林巴类打击乐器以及木管与哨片，以分乐章结构组织不同氛围与织体——从急促而轻柔的打击乐到无人机段落再到近似自由爵士的管乐爆发，最终回归金属质感的环境声响。第二张聚焦吉他，特别是非常规调律的声学吉他在环境中自然互动，巴拉托维奇与斯潘皮纳托的二重奏以稀疏的呼应展开对话，环境中的门声与快门声成为偶然的层次。拉斯特独奏作品同样以两部分的吉他线条呈现。两张作品均体现了芬兰实验音乐场景对即兴、空间感与声音物质性的关注。

items.body: The German duo Arnte and Schmoun—formerly active together as Nordschlacht and Ugh, but having operated as Pyrroline for years—are releasing their fifth album, “Ambiguity”. The work appears inspired by the world we live in and, above all, by the impact of various events on the human psyche. Musically, this translates into 12 tracks that immediately reveal the signature Pyrroline sound. The group remains closely linked to the musical legacy of early Skinny Puppy. Hovering somewhere between sophisticated EBM and atmospheric Dark-Electro, this new opus once again succeeds in captivating the listener. A dark, frenzied atmosphere is established, underpinned by complex percussion. At times, the mood is somewhat tormented, yet that is precisely the strength of certain tracks. The polished production features a wealth of sounds and subtle effects, layered with ghostly vocals. Here and there, female vocals appear, adding a touch of cold sensuality. One of the tracks also features a collaboration with TC75. “Ambiguity” may not be the band’s strongest album—their previous release, “Struggling”, was a masterpiece, after all—but it remains a powerful record from a group that, in my opinion, continues to be somewhat underrated. (Rating:8). Side-Line reported on the album when Pyrroline announced “Ambiguity” in June 2026. The label lists twelve tracks and issued the record as a Digipak CD and digitally. Listen to “Eventually”: Eventually by PYRROLINE About Pyrroline Pyrroline is a German electro-industrial and old-school EBM project built around Arnte on vocals and Schmoun on synths and chants. Discogs lists the duo as a dark electro group based in Germany. The project records for Electro Aggression Records, the label founded in 2011 that concentrates on old-school EBM and electronic body music. The recorded run starts with “Behind The Horizon” in 2010 and “Ruins Outlast” in 2013. Side-Line reviewed the CD album “In The Dawn Of Freedom” in September 2017 and the double CD “Struggling” in May 2021. The single “Relentless” followed in 2023 and a remix collection in 2024. “Ambiguity” runs twelve tracks and shipped on 17 July 2026. Tino Claus of TC75 contributes guest vocals to “Relentless”, and the duo wrote, produced and performed the album themselves. The label released the video for “Day 45”, the ninth track, on 25 August 2026.
items._cn_summary: 德国二人组Pyrroline发行第五张专辑《Ambiguity》，延续早期Skinny Puppy式的工业电子脉络，在精致EBM与氛围暗潮之间游走。十二首作品以复杂打击乐为骨架，叠加幽暗人声、幽灵般的音效层与偶尔出现的女声献声，营造出黑暗而近乎狂躁的听觉场域。制作精良，音色层次丰富，TC75客串其中一条作品。乐评认为该作虽不及前作《Struggling》那般堪称杰作，仍属有力之作，该组合在同类中评价偏低，值得更多关注。整体而言，这是一张延续风格血脉的暗潮/EBM佳作，氛围营造与声音设计扎实，但对熟悉该流派的听众而言缺乏显著突破。
